All five literals retired. send.repeater / send.intruder / send.organizer now install through useSendShortcuts (lib/actions.ts), which reads useChord against the registry; proxy.forward and proxy.toggleIntercept read useChord in pages/intercept.tsx; repeater.send reads useChord in pages/repeater.tsx. grep for useHotkeys(" with a literal chord returns nothing. Pinned structurally by src/lib/keymap-installed.test.ts, which asserts every rebindable id appears in a useChord("<id>") call in both directions and that the six retired literals never return, with a positive control on the corpus size. tsc --noEmit clean; bun test src/lib 151 pass / 0 fail. NOTE for the audit: the docstring at lib/shortcuts.ts:19-20 is now true as written.

comments.author: FixMenusHotkeys
comments.text:
SCOPE CORRECTION for the inventory (issue is closed and correctly closed; this is about the numbers in its title).

THE DENOMINATOR IS WRONG. There are 11 rebindable actions, not 10. Verified by importing the module rather than grepping — `REBINDABLE.length === 11`, and `SHORTCUT_ACTIONS.length === 24`. A `grep -c 'rebindable: true' lib/shortcuts.ts` returns 12, which is the trap: the twelfth hit is the docstring at lib/shortcuts.ts:19 quoting the flag name in prose. The eleven are send.repeater, send.intruder, send.organizer, proxy.forward, proxy.toggleIntercept, repeater.send, nav.palette, nav.nextTool, nav.prevTool, view.toggleTheme, help.shortcuts.

THE NUMERATOR IS ALSO WRONG, in the worse direction. Six of the eleven were inert, not five. The five this issue named were installed as literals; the sixth, send.organizer, was installed nowhere at all and was filed separately as burpsy-react-ui-zy6. Anyone reading the two issues side by side gets the right total, but this issue's title alone understates it. The honest headline is '6 of 11 rebindable hotkeys were inert'.

TWO CAUSES, NOT ONE — this matters for how the fix generalises.
1. Dispatch bypassed the registry (5 actions). Each was a page-local `useHotkeys("<literal>", ...)`. The keymap store worked perfectly: setChord wrote, persist stored, announce broadcast, useKeymap re-rendered, the Settings table re-read and reported success. Nothing was broken inside any module. The chord simply was not what any handler was registered against.
2. Dispatch did not exist (1 action). send.organizer had no call site of any kind.

ROOT CAUSE COMMON TO BOTH, and the reason this was able to ship: nothing tied the registry to the dispatch sites. The declaration lived in lib/shortcuts.ts, the store in lib/keymap.ts, and the handlers in five different page files, with no test and no type spanning them. Every unit was correct in isolation, which is exactly why unit tests could not have caught it and why the fix includes src/lib/keymap-installed.test.ts — a structural test over the source corpus asserting the wiring in both directions. That test is the durable part of this fix; the six call-site edits are not.

SCOPE ESTIMATE, if this had to be re-done from scratch: small. The store, the validation, the duplicate detection and the Settings UI were all already correct and needed no changes. The work was one 60-line hook, five call-site edits, and the structural test. Roughly a third of the effort was the test.

title: session: cookie jar is never populated from proxy traffic, though the page's empty state says it is
description:
## Claim
The session cookie jar is never populated from proxy traffic, and the Session page's empty-state copy tells the operator that it is.

## Burp-side evidence
`/root/burp-re/in/extract/resources/Documentation/burp/documentation/desktop/settings/sessions/index.html`:
> "Burp's cookie jar stores all of the cookies issued by websites you visit. The cookie jar is shared between all of Burp's tools. […] By default, the cookie jar is updated based on traffic from the Proxy."

The same page lists Proxy / Intruder / Scanner / Sequencer / Repeater / Extensions as individually selectable monitored tools, with Proxy on by default.

## burpsy-side evidence
`Coordinator.HandleResponse` — the only Set-Cookie absorption entry point — is `internal/session/session.go:954`, calling `jarMgr.AbsorbSetCookie` at `internal/session/session.go:957`.

Its complete set of non-test callers:
- `cmd/burpsy/cli_session.go:343`
- `internal/web/api_session.go:803` (the login-macro path)
- `internal/session/recovery.go:276`
- `internal/crawler/session_gate.go:261`

The proxy is not among them.

Absence-grep with same-directory positive control:
```
$ grep -rin cookie --include=*.go internal/proxy/
(no output)

$ for f in $(ls internal/proxy/*.go | grep -v _test); do printf "%s %s\n" "$(grep -c 'func ' $f)" "$f"; done
3 internal/proxy/alpn.go
5 internal/proxy/h2_relay.go
23 internal/proxy/options.go
53 internal/proxy/proxy.go
6 internal/proxy/tls_dial.go
3 internal/proxy/tls_peek.go
20 internal/proxy/ws.go
```
Every file in the package is greppable (113 funcs matched), so the zero-hit cookie grep is a real absence, not a NUL-byte read failure.

## The false copy
`internal/web/ui/src/pages/session.tsx:1021`, the empty-jar detail text:
> "The jar is attached and empty: no Set-Cookie has been absorbed yet. Run a login macro, or **send authenticated traffic through the proxy**."

The first clause is true. The second describes a code path that does not exist. This is the part worth fixing first even if the absorption work is scheduled later — the copy currently sends the operator to do something that cannot work.

## Classification
CAPABILITY GAP, plus a false disclosure in shipped UI copy.

## What an operator cannot do
Browse the target logged-in through the proxy and have subsequent tool requests carry the session — the jar stays empty while the UI says their browsing should have filled it.
acceptance_criteria: A response passing through the proxy with a Set-Cookie header results in that cookie appearing in GET /api/session/cookies, covered by a test that drives a response through the proxy path rather than calling HandleResponse directly. If proxy absorption is deliberately declined instead, session.tsx:1021 no longer tells the operator to send traffic through the proxy.
close_reason: Fixed in d44f352. proxy.ProxyConfig.WithCookieJar attaches the session coordinator and Server.record absorbs every Set-Cookie from the raw response bytes - the single funnel all capture sites in internal/proxy go through (HTTP/1, h2 relay, WS handshake). Coordinator.AbsorbResponseCookies takes bytes rather than a header map because HandleResponse's map[string]string can hold only ONE of a response's Set-Cookie lines - a defect the audit did not mention and which affected every existing absorption call site. Wired in cmd/burpsy/main.go:438. The disclosure was NOT the bug: the copy is now true. Second half per the house standard - the coordinator records absorption sources and counts responses/Set-Cookies offered, and /api/session/cookies projects absorbing_from, responses_observed, set_cookies_absorbed with a three-branch empty hint (nothing feeds the jar / nothing has arrived / N arrived and carried none). Those were one indistinguishable state, which is how the false advice shipped. Mutation: removing the absorb call in record() fails TestProxiedTrafficFillsTheSessionCookieJar (real traffic through a real listener); narrowing hdr.Values to hdr.Get fails TestAbsorbResponseCookiesTakesEverySetCookieLine 'absorbed 1 Set-Cookie lines, want 2'. UI half open: session.tsx:1021 copy is now accurate, and the three new fields let the page distinguish the three states.

comments.author: FixBackendTruth
comments.text:
SCOPE NOTE for the inventory (issue is closed/done, this is calibration).

Roughly 2x the filed scope, and the extra half was not visible from the audit's evidence.

The audit's fix — 'call the absorption entry point from the proxy' — was one line and correct. Two things it could not have seen made it bigger:

1. Coordinator.HandleResponse, the entry point the audit identified, takes 'hdrs map[string]string'. A map keyed by header name cannot hold a response's Set-Cookie headers: a login that sets a session cookie AND a CSRF cookie sends two lines and the map holds one. So wiring the proxy to that entry point would have shipped a jar that silently drops half of every real login. That forced a new bytes-taking method (AbsorbResponseCookies + a textproto head parse) rather than a call to the existing one. This is a LATENT DEFECT IN ALL FOUR PRE-EXISTING CALLERS (cli_session.go:343, web/api_session.go:803, session/recovery.go:276, crawler/session_gate.go:261) — they each build that map themselves from an already-parsed response, so the loss happens before HandleResponse is entered and is invisible at those sites. NOT FIXED by me; those paths still use the map. Possibly worth its own issue.

2. The house standard on empty-vs-unmeasured made the honest half comparable in size to the fix. Absorbing cookies makes session.tsx:1021's copy true, but an empty jar still rendered identically to a jar nothing watches. That needed absorption-source registration plus two counters on the Coordinator and a three-branch hint on /api/session/cookies.

WHERE THE FIX LANDED, which the audit did not specify: not at a per-protocol capture site but in proxy.Server.record — the single funnel every capture site in the package goes through (HTTP/1, the h2 relay's rendered copy, the WebSocket handshake). One call covers all three and a site added later inherits it. Worth knowing for any future 'hook the proxy path' issue: record() is the seam.

REMAINING (UI, not mine): session.tsx:1021 copy is now accurate as written, so no edit is strictly required — but the page cannot yet distinguish the three states the API now reports (absorbing_from empty / responses_observed 0 / N observed and none carried a cookie). Small: read three new fields, pick one of three strings.

title: history: the three Search modifier checkboxes have no search field and are applied to the DSL query box
description:
VERIFIED against HEAD by AuditProxy (Proxy-screen parity audit, 2026-08-27).

DECORATIVE CONTROL. The three "Search modifiers" checkboxes in HTTP history's
"More filters" popover have no search field to modify. Their value never leaves
the browser, and the text they operate on is the DSL query box.

## burpsy-side evidence

There is exactly ONE text input on the page:

  pages/history.tsx:888-892
    aria-label="Filter history"
    placeholder="host = api.example AND status >= 400"
    value={term} onChange={... setTerm ...}

`term` has two consumers:

  1. pages/history.tsx:417  const {data} = useHistory(debouncedTerm, limit)
     -> sent to the server as the typed query DSL.

  2. pages/history.tsx:481-503  the `searchMatcher` memo, built from
     `debouncedTerm` and the three checkbox states (searchCase :380,
     searchRegex :381, searchNegate :382).

The matcher is then applied client-side at pages/history.tsx:578-586 against

  `${row.method} ${row.host} ${row.path} ${row.mime ?? ""} ${row.notes ?? ""}`

There is no handler to reach: the checkbox values are consumed entirely inside
the component and never appear in a request body. Nothing on the Go side reads
them.

## What the operator gets

With the box holding its documented content -- a DSL expression, per the
placeholder -- the three controls are worse than absent:

* "Regular expression" (:1156) compiles `host ~ "api" and status = 200` as a
  RegExp (:489) and tests it against the row fields. It matches nothing, the
  table empties, and the status line at :1103-1107 reports
  `no match for search` for a search the operator never typed.

* "Negative match" (:1157-1161) alone inverts a predicate that is false for
  every row (`hit === searchNegate`, :585), so every row is kept: a silent
  no-op that still adds "search (inverted)" to activeFilterNames (:529).

* "Case sensitive" (:1155) behaves as labelled only when the box holds a bare
  word rather than a query.

The hint at :1165-1169 documents which FIELDS are searched and never states
WHICH STRING is searched, so nothing on screen discloses the collision.

Checked and NOT the bug: the branch at :483-486 is convoluted but correct for
every combination -- case-only and negate-only both reach the plain substring
matcher. The defect is the shared input, not the predicate.

## Burp-side evidence

proxyHttpSearchCaseSensitiveCheckbox, proxyHttpSearchRegexCheckbox,
proxyHttpSearchNegativeMatchCheckbox -- all three declared in BurpClass9693.java
(/root/burp-re/out/ui_report/setname_inventory.tsv). In Burp they modify a
DEDICATED search field inside the filter popover, separate from every other
filter control. Burp has no combined filter-expression/search input.

## Classification

CAPABILITY GAP (no search field exists) with an active correctness failure.

## What an operator cannot do

Search history by substring or regex at all -- and if they tick the modifiers
while a DSL query is in the box, the table empties and blames a filter they
never set.

## Shape of the work

Add the search field the modifiers belong to, as a second input in the popover
next to the three checkboxes, leaving the top-bar box as the DSL statement.
Renaming the labels instead would leave a control that still empties the table.
acceptance_criteria: History has a search input distinct from the DSL query box; Case sensitive / Regular expression / Negative match apply only to that input; a DSL query in the top-bar box is unaffected by the three checkboxes; an invalid regex is reported in place rather than emptying the table.
close_reason: Closed

comments.author: openhands
comments.text:
Fixed in fc28efe (branch ui-react-comparison).

The popover now has the dedicated search field Burp's modifiers belong to (the issue's 'Shape of the work' verbatim):

- internal/web/ui/src/lib/history-search.ts (new): compileHistorySearch(text, {caseSensitive, regex}) — pure compile step. Empty/whitespace text means no search is active, whatever the checkboxes hold; regex mode compiles the field as a pattern (RegExp with the case flag); an invalid regex returns {matcher: null, error} so the page can report it in place instead of emptying the table; plain-text mode treats regex metacharacters as literals (String.includes semantics).
- pages/history.tsx: new 'Search for' input in the Search modifiers group, above the checkboxes; the matcher memo compiles from it (own 260ms debounce) instead of the DSL box, so the top-bar box is again purely the server-evaluated query and the three checkboxes cannot touch it (acceptance criterion). Negative match stays an exact inversion at the row predicate (hit === negate). The active-filters line names the needle: search "…" (optionally '(inverted)'), so an empty table names the filter that emptied it. 'Show all' clears the field too.
- Hint text now states which STRING is searched and that the modifiers apply only to this field — the disclosure the issue found missing.

Tests: src/lib/history-search.test.ts (9 cases: empty field inert under all modifier combinations, whitespace-only, case-insensitive default, case-sensitive, regex pattern semantics incl. dot-as-wildcard, regex+case flag, invalid regex → error + null matcher, metacharacters literal in plain-text mode, negation inversion table). bun lib suite: 193 pass / 0 fail (was 184). tsc clean, vite build OK. Go untouched — the old controls never left the browser; internal/web still green (6.3s).

title: ui: the message editor has no context menu and no Actions menu — no send-to from inside a request or response
description:
## Claim
Right-clicking inside a request or response pane in burpsy opens the browser's own menu. There is no burpsy context menu and no "Actions" button anywhere in the message editor, so every send-to / copy / scope action must be reached from the table row above instead.

## Burp-side evidence
- `tools/message-editor/index.html` (Burp 2026.7.1 bundled docs, in `/root/burp-re/in/extract/resources/Documentation/burp/documentation/desktop/`), Raw tab: *"You can access a wide range of context-specific actions for both requests and responses either from the **Actions** menu or by **right-clicking anywhere on the relevant message**."*
- `tools/proxy/intercept-messages.html`: *"You can also right-click to access different context menus in the message editor, or the list of intercepted messages."*
- `tools/context-menu.html` is the canonical universal item list; Burp applies it to editors as well as tables.
- Spec `BURP_SUITE_UI_UX_SPECIFICATION.md` section 5.1: the Send-To matrix is *"Invoked via Right-Click on any HTTP Message editor or History table row"*.

## burpsy-side evidence
- `burpsy-go/internal/web/ui/src/ui/editor.tsx` — absence grep `grep -c ContextMenu ui/editor.tsx` -> **0**. Same-file positive control: `grep -c import ui/editor.tsx` -> **14**. `file ui/editor.tsx` -> `JavaScript source, Unicode text, UTF-8 text` (no NUL byte, so the ugrep/NUL trap does not apply).
- `ui/editor.tsx:212,223` declares an `actions?: ReactNode` toolbar slot. **No caller passes it**: `grep -rn -A9 '<HttpEditor' pages/ ui/ | grep 'actions='` exits 1 across all 21 `<HttpEditor>` usages (`grep -rn '<HttpEditor' pages/ ui/ | wc -l` -> 21).
- The editor toolbar is Wrap / Copy / Save only (`ui/editor.tsx:323-344`).
- The components needed already exist: `ui/menu.tsx:54` `ContextMenu({groups, children})` and `lib/actions.ts:782-834` `menu(exchange, extra)` returning `MenuGroup[]`.

## Classification
CAPABILITY GAP.

## What an operator cannot do
Read a response in the History or Repeater detail pane, right-click it, and send it to Repeater / Intruder / Comparer, copy its URL or curl, or add its host to scope — the highest-frequency gesture in Burp. The selection codecs bound in the editor keymap (`ui/editor.tsx:143-170`, Burp's "Convert selection") are likewise reachable only by keystroke, with no menu entry to discover them from.
acceptance_criteria: Right-clicking anywhere in a request or response pane in History, Repeater, Site map and Intercept opens burpsy's own menu carrying the exchange actions from lib/actions.ts menu(); the same groups are also reachable from a visible Actions control in the editor toolbar.
close_reason: 63e101b8164900cbcd08697a60c61cda3dcab2d5. HttpEditor takes a menuGroups prop and renders the groups in two places: a right-click ContextMenu on the message body (Radix Trigger asChild, so no wrapper element is added to the editor-shell grid) and a visible Actions button in the toolbar via DropdownMenu. Wired with useExchangeActions().menu(exchange) on History (both panes), Site map (both panes), Scanner advisory (both panes), the WebSocket handshake pair, Repeater (keyed on result.exchange_id, since a draft is not an exchange until sent), and Intercept (its own heldMenu, because a held message has no exchange). Also closes the second half of the acceptance criteria: Burp's Convert-selection codecs are now menu entries running the same transformSelection path as the ctrl+U/H/B chords, each row showing its chord, plus Find-in-message. They are enabled/disabled off a real CodeMirror updateListener rather than a render-time read, so the disabled state is not a lie. The Render view keeps the browser's own menu on purpose - it is a sandboxed attacker-controlled iframe. tsc --noEmit clean.

comments.author: FixMenusHotkeys
comments.text:
SCOPE ANSWER for the inventory: pf9 was SMALLER than it looks, and it bought more than it asked for. Numbers, since the issue's own census was the thing that made it look big.

THE 21 CALL SITES WERE A RED HERRING. The issue counts 21 `<HttpEditor>` usages (22 now) and observes that none passes `actions`, which reads as 21 places to fix. It is not. The fix is ONE prop on ONE component plus a per-page lookup of the exchange, and only 11 of the 22 sites have an exchange to look up:

  wired (11): history x2, sitemap x2, scanner x2, wshistory handshake x2, repeater x2, intercept x1
  correctly not wired (11): decoder 1, comparer 1, session 1, sequencer 2, matchreplace 2, intruder 2, wshistory frame payload 2

The second group is not a backlog. Those panes hold a token list, a paste buffer, a match/replace preview, a synthesised payload — there is no exchange behind them, so there is no send-to that would not be fabricated. An engineer picking this up should not budget for 22.

IT ALSO FIXED editor.* FOR FREE, WHICH THE ISSUE ONLY MENTIONS IN PASSING. The last line of the issue's evidence notes the selection codecs are 'reachable only by keystroke, with no menu entry to discover them from'. That turned out to be the cheaper and arguably higher-value half: the codec entries live INSIDE HttpEditor, so they need no caller cooperation at all, and every one of the 22 editors now has a right-click menu and an Actions button carrying URL/HTML/Base64 encode+decode and Find-in-message, each row displaying its chord so the menu teaches the keyboard. That includes all 11 editors with no exchange — the Sequencer's token pane and the Decoder's input got the most useful thing in this commit and are not mentioned anywhere in the issue.

ONE THING THAT WAS HARDER THAN IT LOOKS, worth knowing before anyone touches this again: the codec entries' enabled/disabled state cannot be read when the menu is built. `groups` is a prop evaluated at render, not a callback invoked on open, so a selection made after that render would leave every codec row stale — enabled and doing nothing, or disabled and refusing to. It needs a real `EditorView.updateListener` pushing selection-emptiness into React state. Anyone 'simplifying' that back to a direct `cmViewRef.current.state.selection` read reintroduces the bug silently, because the menu still looks right.

AND ONE TRAP AVOIDED: the Actions trigger is a bare `<button>`, not the codebase's `IconButton`. IconButton wraps its button in a Radix Tooltip, so using it would stack two `asChild` layers on one DOM node and merge two sets of handlers onto it. app.tsx's menu bar uses a bare button for the same reason. Noted in the code.

REVISED SIZE: small-to-medium, and it is a single shared fix, not 21. The P1 is justified on frequency, not on cost.

title: auditqueue: "Show insertion points" only ever expands the first row
description:
## Claim

The Audit queue's "Show insertion points" button only ever expands the **first** row. For every other
item in the queue it appears to do nothing, so an operator reads "no insertion points were recorded"
where the truth is "this control cannot show you them".

## burpsy side

`burpsy-go/internal/web/ui/src/pages/auditqueue.tsx:122`

    onClick={() => setExpanded(expanded === null ? (d.items[0]?.seq ?? null) : null)}

`expanded` is a single `number | null` (`:28`), and the render gate is
`expanded === item.seq && item.insertion_points?.length` (`:101`). The button is page-level, in
`toolbar-end` below the table (`:118-126`) — there is no per-row toggle and no way to reach
`d.items[1]` or later. The label is unconditional ("Show insertion points"), so it does not disclose
that it means row 1.

The data is present for every row: `item.insertion_points` is per-item on the wire
(`lib/data.auditqueue.ts`), carrying `kind`, `name`, `status`, `detail`.

## Burp side

`auditItemsTableInsertionPointsViewToggle` is **per row** in Burp's Audit items table — `map_root.tsv`
class `burp.Zub5` (`auditItemsTableInsertionPointsViewToggle`, `Insertion points`) and `burp.Zrz9`
(`auditItemsTableInsertionPointsView`). The tree it opens is scoped to the selected item
(`burp.Zr_x`: `auditItemsTableInsertionPointsName`, `auditItemsTableInsertionPointsStatusText`).

## Classification

CAPABILITY GAP, and specifically a wrong-result one: the control silently under-reports rather than
refusing.

## What an operator cannot do

Find out which insertion points the audit chose, or why one was skipped, on any queue item except the
first — which is the question the Audit queue exists to answer.
acceptance_criteria: Insertion points can be expanded for any row in the queue independently (per-row toggle or multi-select expansion state), verified on a queue with 2+ items where a later item has insertion points.
close_reason: Done in 6d0b20e. The page-level button is gone; each row now has its own toggle. The old handler was setExpanded(expanded === null ? (d.items[0]?.seq ?? null) : null) — it could only ever reach d.items[0], and because the render gate is 'expanded === item.seq && item.insertion_points?.length', clicking it on any other row produced no change and read as 'no insertion points recorded' rather than 'this control cannot show you them'. On a queue whose stated purpose is that bounded work is reported and never dropped, that was silent under-reporting, which is why P1 was right. The new button carries its own count so the number is visible without expanding, and a row with zero points gets it DISABLED rather than hidden — hiding it would leave an operator unable to tell 'this item recorded none' from 'this item has some and the toggle is broken again', which is the exact confusion being fixed. The expanded panel also now names which seq it belongs to, since with a per-row toggle there is more than one row it could have come from. tsc clean. dist/app.js deliberately not rebuilt yet: three agents are mid-flight on other files and I rebuild once when they land, so this does not reach a browser until then.

title: scanner: only 4 of Burp's 78 scan-config keys exist; insertion points and check selection are unrepresentable
description:
burpsy's `scanner.BuiltInConfig` has **4 knobs**. Burp's 29 shipped configurations set **78
functional leaf keys across 15 sections**. That is **4/78 (5%)**, spanning **2/15 sections**.

## Re-derived, not inherited

`docs/parity/W0-burp-denominators.md` states it was reconstructed and not re-derived. I re-derived it
from `/root/burp-re/in/extract/resources/BuiltInConfigs` (29 files, confirmed):

| Figure | W0 said | Re-derived | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| BuiltInConfigs files | 29 | 29 | confirmed |
| total leaf keys | 83 | 84 | off by one |
| `description.*` metadata | 6 | 6 | confirmed |
| functional keys | 77 | **78** | corrected |
| sections | 20 | **15** | W0 overstated by 5 |

Use 78 and 15. The conclusion is unchanged and the correction is small, but the numbers get quoted.

## The two sections that are entirely unrepresentable

**`scanner/insertion_point_types` — 8 keys.** Controls WHERE the scanner injects:

    insert_url_params, insert_body_params, insert_cookies, insert_http_headers,
    insert_param_name, insert_url_path_filename, insert_url_path_folders, insert_entire_body

**`scanner/issues_reported` — 9 keys.** Controls WHICH checks run:

    scan_type_passive, scan_type_light_active, scan_type_medium_active,
    scan_type_intrusive_active, scan_type_javascript_analysis,
    scan_only_selected_issues, select_individual_issues, selected_issues,
    store_issues_within_queue_items

A scanner whose insertion points and check selection cannot be expressed is not a configurable
scanner. This is the single largest capability gap on the Burp side of the comparison, and it is not
a UI gap — there is no field to bind a control to.

## What burpsy's 4 keys cover

`ConsecutiveCheckFailuresToAbandonUnit`, `ConsecutiveUnitFailuresToFailItem`,
`PauseSessionAfterFailedItems` land in `scanner/error_handling` (5 keys); `MaximumAuditTimeMinutes` is
`scanner/audit_optimization/maximum_crawl_and_audit_time` (7 keys). Every one was verified present in
Burp's JSON — the transcription is honest, it is just tiny.

Note what `error_handling` is missing even within a section burpsy touches:
`number_of_follow_up_passes` and `pause_task_failed_audit_item_percentage`.

## Why this is P1 and should be split

Do NOT take this as one task. `issues_reported` is the higher value half: `settings.tsx` already has
~21 audit-check-family switches wired to `ScanConfig`, so burpsy has *a* check-selection mechanism —
it is simply not Burp's shipped vocabulary and cannot load a Burp configuration. Reconciling those two
is a smaller, well-defined job than building insertion-point control from nothing.

`insertion_point_types` is the deeper one: it needs the audit engine to be told which insertion point
classes to enumerate, which touches `internal/scanner`'s point generation rather than a config struct.

## Constraint inherited from the existing code

`builtInConfigKeys` is deliberately the single description of what a shipped configuration can change,
read by both `Apply` and `BuiltInConfig.Keys` so a chooser can tell an operator what each config does.
Any new key must go through that table, not around it.
acceptance_criteria: scanner/issues_reported and scanner/insertion_point_types are representable, a Burp-shipped configuration can be loaded without silently dropping keys, and builtInConfigKeys remains the single description of what a config changes.
close_reason: Closed

comments.author: openhands
comments.text: Implemented in burpsy-go commit 6d61865. The scanner now honours 18 of Burp's 78 scan-config keys plus reports 3 as deliberately unapplied: AuditConfig.InsertionKinds feeds point enumeration (overlay names the section -> full Burp-shaped base set, add/remove per key, 'none' sentinel when all off); issues_reported gates narrow the per-run check set via enabledChecksUnder (passive/DOM families, collapsed active tiers, tier-collapse disclosed in audit reply as audit_level_notes); store_issues_within_queue_items=false skips queue attachment; ParseBurpConfig reads Burp's own nested config files (scanner.{insertion_point_types,issues_reported,error_handling,audit_optimization}) and -scan-config /path/to/config.json loads them; ApplyWithReport returns unapplied keys, echoed by the audit reply (unapplied_keys) and configs API; web config view grew the new fields (null = inherit). Tests: field/row invariant updated for field-less rows, new kind-mapping + overlay add/remove + gate-narrowing + parser tests; full Go suite green (scanner package 356s, flaky stored-row test passes on rerun).

title: intercept: right-click Forward/Drop act on the previously selected message
description:
`burpsy-go/internal/web/ui/src/pages/intercept.tsx` (~line 617) gives the held-message table a
right-click menu whose Forward and Drop items act on the *previously selected* message, not the one
the operator right-clicked.

## The code

```tsx
menuGroups={(row) => [{ id: "intercept", actions: [
  { id: "forward", label: "Forward", icon: Send, shortcut: "Ctrl+F",
    onSelect: () => { setSelectedId(row.id); setTimeout(forward, 0); } },
  { id: "drop", label: "Drop", icon: Trash2, danger: true,
    onSelect: () => { setSelectedId(row.id); setTimeout(drop, 0); } },
]}]}
```

`forward` is defined at line 400 and closes over `selected` (line 376, derived from `selectedId`) and
over `raw`, the edit buffer. `setSelectedId` schedules a state update; it does not rewrite the
`forward` function that already exists. `setTimeout` then re-invokes *that same closure*, so it still
reads the pre-click `selected` and the pre-click `raw`.

## Three distinct failures

1. **Wrong message forwarded.** Right-click a held message that is not the current selection, pick
   Forward: the previously selected message is forwarded, and the success toast names that one
   ("Held message #N forwarded"), so the log agrees with the wrong outcome.

2. **Silent no-op.** With nothing selected yet, `if (!selected) return` at line 401 makes the item do
   nothing at all — no error, no toast.

3. **Wrong payload, which is the serious one.** `raw` is the edit buffer belonging to the *old*
   selection. The effect that resets it (lines 380-383) keys on `selectedId` and runs after commit,
   so the stale closure sends the previous message's bytes as this message's payload. An operator who
   had been editing message A and right-click-forwards message B sends A's edited bytes to B's
   destination.

`drop` (line 414) has the same stale-closure problem, without the payload hazard: it drops the
previously selected message.

## Why this is P1 rather than P2

This is the interception surface. Its whole purpose is that the operator controls exactly which bytes
reach the server, and "the control acted on a message other than the one you pointed at, and told you
it succeeded" defeats that. It also cannot be caught by reading the toast, because the toast reports
the action that actually happened.

## Fix

`setTimeout(…, 0)` is the signal, not the fix — it is there because the author noticed state was not
applied yet. Do not wait for state; pass the target explicitly. Extract the id-taking forms:

```tsx
const forwardMessage = (id: number, body: string) => { … };
const dropMessage = (id: number) => { … };
```

and have both the existing buttons and the menu items call those. The menu item then needs to decide
what `body` means for a row that is not the selected one — the honest answer is the row's own
unedited `raw`, since there is no edit buffer for it.

## Verification

`npx tsc --noEmit` is exit 0. The `onActivate` additions on the same two `VirtualTable` pages are
correct and match `table.tsx:435`; only the `setTimeout` handlers are affected.
acceptance_criteria: Right-clicking an unselected held message and choosing Forward forwards THAT message's id and bytes; with nothing previously selected it still works; a test covers forward-from-menu on a row other than the current selection.
close_reason: Done in ecfe2bd. DustyCanyon's extraction was the right fix — forwardMessage(id, body, fixCL) and dropMessage(id) taking their target explicitly instead of closing over selected/raw — and that is what landed, reapplied onto HEAD's formatting so the ~600-line reindentation it arrived wrapped in did not land with it. git diff and git diff -w on the file are now identical at 63 lines: every changed line is a real change. Their working copy is preserved (scratchpad/intercept.tsx.dustycanyon-worktree-1657, sha256 72d2397b1fc3) and the substitution was announced in msg 1517 before the operator authorised the takeover. Also fixed the regression their version carried: fixContent_length was dropped by JSON.stringify so the handler decoded FixContentLength as false and Content-Length correction was silently off for EVERY forward, including the toolbar path that worked before; and the menu hardcoded true where the operator's toggle belonged, which would have had two forward paths disagreeing about whether they rewrite a header. The menu passes row.raw, not the edit buffer, deliberately: there is no edit buffer for an unselected row. tsc clean tree-wide; full suite exit 0, 37 packages.

title: discover: the ffuf content-discovery engine has no console surface
description:
VERIFIED, and sharper than the original issue. The original said 'No content discovery functionality' and 'Discover tab is docs only'. Both halves were wrong in opposite directions.

WHAT EXISTS: ffuf-backed content discovery is fully built in Go — internal/extscan/ffuf.go, internal/web/api_discovery.go, the /api/discovery route registered at internal/web/server.go:817, discoveryRuns state at server.go:102-104, and tests in api_discovery_test.go and route_manifest_test.go. It is reachable from the CLI (cmd/burpsy/cli_extscan.go).

WHAT IS MISSING: nothing in the console calls it. `grep -rn 'api/discovery' internal/web/ui/src` returns zero hits. An operator using the web console cannot launch a content-discovery run, see one in progress, or read its results.

WHY discover.tsx IS NOT THE GAP: the original conflated two different Burp features. Burp's DISCOVER *tab* is a links farm (Web Security Academy, manual, videos, forum); burpsy replaced it with a reference hub deliberately, and discover.tsx's module doc argues that case at length. Burp's 'Discover content' is a separate engagement tool reached by right-clicking a target. This issue is about the second one. Do not 'fix' it by changing discover.tsx into a links page.

WHY P1: this is the same failure class as matchreplace-never-wired — a complete engine, tests passing, reported as delivered, that no user can reach. Backend coverage is exactly what makes it invisible.
acceptance_criteria: A console surface can start an ffuf discovery run against a chosen target, shows it running, and renders its results; the route appears in dist/app.js as well as server.go.
close_reason: Done in 03ae0b7. Added lib/data.discovery.ts (typed wire shapes + useDiscoveryRuns/useStartDiscovery), pages/contentdiscovery.tsx, and a Content discovery leaf under Target next to the site map — where Burp opens 'Discover content' from — leaving pages/discover.tsx untouched, since the two Burp features only share a word. The page renders looked, outcome, counts.out_of_scope and the server's verbatim summary, so 'swept and found nothing' and 'never swept' get different panels; the argv is shown per run because these requests bypass burpsy and appear in no history row; and when ffuf is not allowlisted the reason replaces the form rather than showing an empty table. Also added internal/web/ui_route_reachability_test.go, the gate that would have caught this class: every manifest route's path must appear in the console source, with uiRouteExempt (reasons) and uiRouteMissingSurface (issue ids) and a third test that fails if a listed gap gains a caller. Its first run found /api/intercept/drop-all, filed as burpsy-react-ui-t6f. NOTE: the first version of that test passed its own mutation test because it matched the route named in a doc comment; comments are now stripped and the mutation test verified red-on-mutation, green-on-restore. NOT rebuilt: dist/app.js, because another agent has five UI files uncommitted — the page is source-only and reaches no browser until someone rebuilds.

title: WS fragment reassembly not supported
description:
## What's missing
wsHoldable() refuses fragmented frames (FIN clear / continuation opcode). Burp reassembles fragments.

## Evidence
- internal/proxy/ws.go:410-431 — wsHoldable() documentation states this gap
- wsHoldable() returns false for fragments

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Buffer continuation frames until FIN
- [ ] Hold complete reassembled message
- [ ] Apply match/replace to reassembled payload

Found by: BlueBison (code grep ws.go:410)
close_reason: Done in c3de955: wsFragments reassembles continuation frames so a multi-frame message can be held, edited and dropped as one message. Control frames still interleave per RFC 6455 s5.4; RSV1 tracked only on a message's first frame per s6.1. Tests in internal/proxy/ws_*_test.go. Verified present in HEAD; full suite exit 0, 37 packages.

title: WS match/replace rules not implemented
description:
## What's missing
WebSocket match/replace rules. HTTP match/replace exists (internal/matchreplace/) but no WS-specific rule engine.

## Evidence
- internal/matchreplace/ — only HTTP request/response rules
- internal/proxy/ws.go:wsHoldable() — refuses compressed/fragmented frames
- No WS match/replace API endpoint in internal/web/

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] WS frame payload matching (literal + regex)
- [ ] WS frame payload replacement
- [ ] API endpoint for WS match/replace rules
- [ ] UI: Match & Replace tab → WebSocket section

Found by: BlueBison (code grep)
close_reason: Done in 6e98c74: matchreplace gained TargetWebSocketToServer/ToClient and DirWebSocketToServer/ToClient, applied in the relay via wsMatchReplaceDirection, ordered BEFORE interception to mirror proxy.go. The if-chain in targetsDir was replaced with a sentinel-sized table so a new target cannot silently fall into the else branch; fixContentLength is skipped for WS directions. Note: without the wsNeedsFrames change in the same commit, WS rules would have installed, reported success and rewritten nothing.

title: network: no DNS address-family preference — a dual-stack host behind one-family routing dials the unreachable address (mr83 part 2)
description:
Split out of burpsy-react-ui-mr83, which bundles three independent dial-path changes. This is the second.

## The gap
Burp: settings/network/dns.html:49-65 — system default, Prefer IPv4, or Prefer IPv6, "because routing restrictions may permit only one family."

burpsy offered system-versus-named-resolver selection plus exact hostname overrides, and returned the resolver addresses unfiltered. Address ordering was entirely the system resolver's.

## The operator loses
Any engagement on a host reachable only over one family. A dual-stack target behind IPv4-only routing can resolve to an AAAA first, and burpsy dials the unreachable address. There was no setting that fixes it; the only workaround was the per-hostname override table, applied one address at a time.

## Fix
Resolution.Family — system (default), ipv4, ipv6. A filter over the resolver answer, not a resolver rewrite: a per-family query (AAAA rather than A) can be answered differently by a split-horizon resolver than a filtered answer to the question the operator actually asked, and the engagement own DNS is the thing that knows. RFC 6555 filtered AAAA exists for deployments that want it; a security tool should not be one by default.

- Applied on BOTH dial paths (the raw sender and the typed transport Repeater uses). Two paths that disagreed here would be a Repeater send that reached an IPv6-only host and a scanner probe that did not.
- An OVERRIDE is never filtered: the operator named an address, and substituting a different one would be worse than the defect being fixed.
- System costs no lookup — the default hands the hostname to the dialer exactly as before, so the ordinary send pays nothing.
- A family with no address in it is a NAMED failure naming the field to change, not a generic "could not resolve" that would send an operator to the DNS settings instead of the family preference.

## Verification, and an honest limit
The preference is proved by a lookup seam answering with BOTH families, IPv6 first, against a real IPv4 listener: the send reaches the listener, and the listener sees the connection. A mutation removing the preference from the typed transport fails it.

The LIVE pass could not demonstrate the defect on this machine, and the reason is recorded in resolution_family_live_test.go: /etc/hosts gave the name both families with the AAAA first, against an IPv4-only listener, and both family=system and family=ipv4 answered 200 in under 10ms. A direct dial to an unroutable AAAA failed in 0.00s — this host has no IPv6 route at all, so an AAAA dial fails instantly rather than timing out. The defect needs a network that DROPs the AAAA rather than rejecting it, which a loopback cannot provide.
close_reason: A dual-stack target behind IPv4-only routing can resolve to an AAAA first, and burpsy dialled the unreachable address, so a request took the connect timeout to fail on a host that was reachable all along; there was no setting that fixed it and the only workaround was the per-hostname override table. Burp's answer is the resolution-address preference (settings/network/dns.html:49-65), 'because routing restrictions may permit only one family'. Resolution.Family is system/ipv4/ipv6, applied on BOTH dial paths -- the raw sender and the typed transport Repeater uses, because two paths that disagreed would be a Repeater send that reached an IPv6-only host and a scanner probe that did not. It is a filter over the resolver's answer rather than a resolver rewrite: a per-family query can be answered differently by a split-horizon resolver than a filtered answer to the question the operator asked, and the engagement's own DNS is what knows. An override is never filtered, because the operator named an address and substituting another is worse than the defect. System costs no lookup, so an ordinary send pays nothing for a preference nobody set. A family with no address is a named failure pointing at the field to change. The live pass could not demonstrate the defect and the reason is recorded in the test: this host has no IPv6 route, so an AAAA dial fails in 0.00s instead of timing out, and both family=system and family=ipv4 answered 200 in under 10ms against an IPv4-only listener. The selection is proved through a Lookup seam answering with both families, IPv6 first, against a real IPv4 listener: the send reaches the listener and the listener sees the connection. Mutation-checked three ways: a no-op filter, system treated as a filter, and removing the preference from the typed transport -- the third survived the first round of tests and is why the two-family seam exists. Split out of mr83, which stays open for the global SOCKS carrier. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./... green with the test cache cleared, tsc clean, bun test:lib 711/0, check:tokens green, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

title: redirect: a followed chain does not replay the cookies each hop set (mr83 part 1)
description:
Split out of burpsy-react-ui-mr83, which bundles three independent dial-path changes. This is the first.

## The gap
Burp: settings/tools/repeater.html:143-145 -- "If you enable this setting, Burp resubmits any cookies set in the redirect response when it follows the redirection target." burpsy built each hop from the previous REQUEST only, so a login or SSO flow that sets a cookie on its 302 arrived at the destination unauthenticated. The redirect was followed, the cookie was not sent, and the destination returned its login page -- which reads as an application failure rather than a missing cookie, and is the single most common redirect shape in an authenticated tool.

internal/web/repeater_options.go stated the absence plainly, so nothing on screen was wrong. This is the capability plus the option Burp exposes alongside it.

## Fix
- RedirectSettings.ReplayCookies, default OFF (unlike a browser: burpsy sends what an operator wrote, and a target-set credential is not one they asked to send; a target that sets throwaway cookies is the other reason a switch is needed).
- The follower absorbs each hop response Set-Cookie into a jar and adds the jar cookies to the NEXT hop, scoped to the hop own authority and Path.
- A hop that already carries a Cookie header keeps it -- the operator typed it.
- The jar is the SESSION coordinator the Session page shows and the other tools already send from, not a second store, so a login performed by a chain is visible everywhere.

## A real bug the unit tests could not see
repeaterSendOptions.redirectPolicy rebuilt RedirectSettings field by field on a per-send mode override, so ReplayCookies silently dropped to false. The console showed the setting ON, the operator sent with "always", and no cookie was replayed. The field-by-field rebuild is replaced with a copy-and-replace-one-field, and a test asserts on the whole struct so a field added later cannot default to false here.

Live through a real console: replay OFF -- the hop request carries no Cookie and the destination answers "LOGIN PAGE"; replay ON -- the hop request carries Cookie: session=real-session-value and the destination answers "DASHBOARD - authenticated".
close_reason: A login or SSO flow that sets a cookie on its 302 arrived at the destination unauthenticated: the redirect was followed, the cookie was not sent, and the destination returned its login page, which reads as an application failure rather than a missing cookie. Burp exposes the fix as a setting; burpsy had the absence documented, so nothing on screen was wrong. ReplayCookies defaults OFF unlike a browser's, because burpsy sends what an operator wrote and a target-set credential is not something they asked to send. Each hop's Set-Cookie is absorbed and the next hop carries it, scoped to that hop's own authority and Path; a hop that already carries a Cookie header keeps it. The jar is the SESSION coordinator rather than a second store, behind a two-method interface because internal/session imports internal/sender, and it takes the Set-Cookie values rather than response bytes. A real bug the unit tests could not see: repeaterSendOptions.redirectPolicy rebuilt RedirectSettings field by field on a per-send mode override, so ReplayCookies dropped to false -- the console showed the setting ON, the operator sent with 'always', and no cookie was replayed, with every sender test green because they attach their own jar. The rebuild is now copy-and-replace-one-field. Live through a real console against a real login flow: replay off, the hop request carries no Cookie and the destination answers LOGIN PAGE; replay on, the same request carries Cookie: session=real-session-value and the destination answers DASHBOARD. Mutation-checked six ways including removing the absorb, removing the apply, letting the jar replace the operator's own header, never attaching the session jar, and dropping the hop's Path. Split out of mr83, which stays open for the DNS family preference and the global SOCKS carrier. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./... green, tsc clean, bun test:lib 711/0, check:tokens green, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

title: history: the Search box searches five columns of loaded rows, and the default message reading is hard-coded to edited
description:
QA PASS 2026-09-25 — history's Search box searches five columns of the rows already loaded, and the default message reading is hard-coded.

## 1. Search covers five fields, not the data (P2)

**Burp:** tools/proxy/http-history/index.html:136-140 — *"Enter a search term in the Search box to find matching items across all columns. The search applies to the underlying data, regardless of any filters you have applied."* The second sentence is the load-bearing one: the search is over the **capture**, not over the visible page.

**burpsy:** the dedicated search runs over method, host, path, MIME and comment of the rows already fetched (`pages/history.tsx:645-650`), and the page loads at most the newest 2,000 / 5,000 / 10,000 / 50,000 rows (`:423,1284-1295`). The code says so plainly at `:1493-1497`: the search operates over already-loaded rows.

**What the operator loses:** anything outside those five columns and outside the loaded window. A page title, a response header, a request body fragment, a comment on a row older than the cap, or a listener port — none is findable from the Search box, and each has to be reconstructed as a separate DSL filter. The box is labelled Search, sitting next to a Filter button, and the two are documented as different in Burp; here the Search box quietly behaves like a filter over the current page.

**Fix:** make the Search box a server-side query over the store, with the existing DSL as its grammar and the current client-side path kept for the instant narrow case. The API already takes `q` (`api_capture.go`), so this is a UI routing change, not a new search engine. The help text under the box should say which of the two it is.

## 2. The default message reading is not configurable (P3)

**Burp:** `map_root.tsv:20253` — *"Use this setting to choose whether the Proxy history message editor displays auto-modified, manually edited, or original messages by default"*; the neighbouring rows name the persisted key `user_options.proxy.default_display_message`.

**burpsy:** `pages/history.tsx:685-701` hard-codes both `requestVariant` and `responseVariant` to `"edited"`, and resets them to `"edited"` on every selection. No store field, no setting, no API path changes that default.

**What the operator loses:** the ability to make Original or Auto-modified the standing reading. On an engagement where auto-modification is routinely involved, every inspected exchange needs the picker re-clicked, and — worse — the default silently differs from Burp's, so a migrated operator sees a different message than the one their habits expect.

**Fix:** a three-way setting in the editor's own settings, persisted in the workspace store beside the other editor preferences (`editorTabs`, `urlEncodeAsYouType`), defaulting to Burp's own default so the out-of-box reading matches. Small, self-contained, and it removes a difference an operator cannot currently see or change.

title: history/intercept: rules cannot AND/OR, no listener filter, parameterized counts query only, no newline correction on an edited forward
description:
QA PASS 2026-09-25 — four interception/history behaviours Burp has that burpsy does not. Grouped because each is a control the operator is shown or promised, and none of them is a large engine change.

## 1. Interception rules cannot combine with AND or OR (P2)

**Burp:** settings/tools/proxy.html:246-268 — each rule picks AND or OR to combine it with the rules above, and *"Each rule is combined to the rules above in order, using the selected boolean operator."*

**burpsy:** `internal/intercept/intercept.go:722-778` evaluates the enabled list as **first matching rule wins**, and the rule editor (`internal/web/ui/src/pages/intercept.tsx:261-384`) offers field, match, action, comment, enable and ordering — no operator column.

**The operator loses:** any hold condition that is a conjunction. "Hold requests to host A **and** path /admin" is two rules that today behave as an OR (the first that matches decides), so the operator either over-holds or writes a single brittle rule that has to enumerate both facts in one matcher. This is the reason Burp has the boolean column, and it is the most commonly written interception rule after "hold on this host".

**Fix:** an operator field per rule and a left-to-right fold over the enabled list, with the current first-match behaviour as the default when every rule says OR. A test that two-rule conjunction holds only when both facts match, and that the default ordering is unchanged.

## 2. No listener-port filter in HTTP history (P2)

**Burp:** tools/proxy/http-history/filter-settings.html:109-116 — *"Filter by listener - You can show items received on a specific listener port. This can be useful when testing access controls."*

**burpsy:** the Listener port column is rendered (`pages/history.tsx:984-996`) but the complete More-filters surface (`:1499-1555`) has no listener control and no listener query field.

**The operator loses:** isolating one listener's traffic when several receive it. The port is captured and displayed but not filterable, and a column cannot be filtered without reconstructing the predicate as DSL. `tyeo` was closed as a duplicate of `mr4p`, whose close reason implemented only the IP column — so the listener filter was closed without ever being built.

**Fix:** a `listener` filter beside the existing port/protocol axes, a query field for it, and a `tyeo` follow-up note so the duplicate closure is recorded rather than repeated.

## 3. "Parameterized requests" counts only query parameters (P2)

**Burp:** `out/clean/root/Zb2y.java:270-273,450-455` — Burp's SHOW_ONLY_PARAMETERIZED_REQUESTS predicate explicitly accepts `HttpParameterType.URL` **or** `HttpParameterType.BODY`.

**burpsy:** `pages/history.tsx:326-338` deliberately counts query parameters only, applies that as the onlyParameterized filter (`:638-640`), and discloses the limitation in the filter's own help (`:1502-1507`).

**The operator loses:** every body-only parameterized request. A JSON API POST with a body and no query string, a multipart upload, an XML API call — all classified as unparameterized and all dropped when the operator filters to parameterized traffic, which is the filter you use to find attack surface. The disclosure is honest, and the answer is still "the filter does not mean what its name says".

**Fix:** count body parameters the way the grammar already can (`queryParamCount` is path-based; the request body is available in the same projection), or rename the filter to what it measures. The first is correct, because Burp's own semantics are the first.

## 4. No newline correction on a forwarded interception edit (P2)

**Burp:** settings/tools/proxy.html:273-292 — Burp can add a missing blank line after headers and remove trailing newlines from URL-encoded bodies when an **edited** intercepted request is forwarded.

**burpsy:** the interception editor offers only "Fix Content-Length when forwarding" (`pages/intercept.tsx:1155-1160`); `internal/intercept/intercept.go:886-899` applies only `rewriteContentLength`, which changes no newline bytes.

**The operator loses:** a reliable forward after editing. An edit that drops the blank line after headers, or leaves a trailing newline in a form body, produces a request the target may reject — and the failure looks like the application's, not the operator's. Content-Length is fixed automatically; framing is not.

**Fix:** the two corrections Burp names, applied on the release path when the request was edited, each with its own toggle in the interception settings. Both are local byte edits on a message the operator already chose to edit, so neither widens what the proxy can send.

## Why together

Each is a control an operator either cannot find or cannot express, and each is a bounded change: a rule field and a fold, a filter and a query field, a count, two byte-level corrections. They are filed together because they are all "the last mile of an existing surface" rather than missing subsystems — the same shape as the last QA batch, and the same reason an operator would rather have them than not.

title: scanner: an audit item cannot be cancelled, issues carry no time/source, and a single finding cannot be reported with its HTTP evidence
description:
QA PASS 2026-09-25 — the audit queue cannot cancel one item, and the Issues table cannot say where an issue came from or when it was found. Filed together: both are "the data exists, the operator cannot act on it".

## 1. No per-item cancel (P2)

**Burp:** running-scans/results/audit-items/index.html:102-115 — the audit-item context menu provides **Cancel** to stop auditing one item.

**burpsy:** the only accepted audit-item action is `POST /api/scanner/audit-items/{id}/again` (`internal/web/api_scanner_audit_items.go:301-308`), and the row menu offers only "Audit again" (`internal/web/ui/src/pages/auditqueue.tsx:149-162`).

**The operator loses:** the ability to stop one long-running or unwanted item. The options are to wait for it or to disable the enclosing live task, which stops everything including the items that are fine. A crawler that reached a slow or heavily-guarded URL holds a slot and a thread until its own bounds expire, and the queue offers no way to reclaim just that one.

**Fix:** `POST .../{id}/cancel`, wired to the same `Control` the pause/stop path already uses (`internal/intruder/control.go` is the model), with the item's terminal state recorded as cancelled — a distinct state from skipped or errored, because "we stopped this" and "this could not run" are different facts about coverage.

## 2. Issues carry no time, source, or check-kind (P2)

**Burp:** running-scans/results/issues.html:89-118,132-165 lists **Time** and **Source** on every issue and filters by BCheck / Scan check / Extension / manually generated provenance. map_root.tsv:10282-10295 carries the same literals.

**burpsy:** the issue view has `task_id` but omits the finding's timestamp and has no source or check-kind field (`internal/web/api_capture.go:804-851`); the Issues page filters on severity, confidence, false-positive state and free text only, and displays no time, task or check kind (`internal/web/ui/src/pages/scanner.tsx:190-259, 830-872`).

**The operator loses:** the ability to separate a manual finding from a scan's, to tell which of three tasks raised an issue, to filter by check provenance, or to order by when something was found. On a long engagement the issue list is an unordered set of rows from every producer in the project.

**Fix:** project `core.Finding.Timestamp` and the existing task attribution into the issue view, add a source facet (scan check / BCheck / manual, all of which the finding already knows), and render Time and Source as columns. This is a projection and a filter, not a schema change.

## 3. A single finding cannot be reported with its HTTP evidence (P2)

**Burp:** issues.html:195-228 offers **Report selected issues**; report-settings.html:98-111 lets a report include the relevant request/response extract or the full HTTP messages.

**burpsy:** the per-issue Report menu opens whole-scan HTML/JSON/SARIF exports (`internal/web/ui/src/pages/scanner.tsx:455-463`), and report Evidence holds only method, host, path and status — no bytes (`internal/report/report.go:67-73`).

**The operator loses:** a self-contained handoff for one finding. The deliverable an assessor needs is the request that produced it and the response that came back; the available export is scan-wide and metadata-only, so a single-issue report has to be assembled by hand.

**Fix:** a selected-issue report that carries the evidence rows the project already stores — the finding's occurrence already names request and response message ids, and `store.Raw` can read the bytes at export time, so no new storage is required.

## Why together

Each is the same shape: the data is retained (audit-item evidence, finding timestamps, occurrence message ids) and the operator-facing layer drops it. One rendering/projection change per item, and together they are the difference between a queue an operator can steer and one they can only watch.

title: scanner: the audit-queue parity table denies the light-audit pass the same package implemented
description:
QA PASS 2026-09-25 — the audit-queue's own parity table says a light-audit pass does not exist, in the same package that implemented it.

## The contradiction

`burpsy-go/internal/scanner/audit_items.go:145-151` — the table of Burp statuses this engine does not model — says, three times, that there is no light-active pass:

- `LIGHT_AUDITING` — *"there is no light-active pass: every admitted check runs its full probe set or is refused"*
- `LIGHT_AUDITED` — *"there is no light-active pass, so no item can finish having had only one"*
- `NOT_LIGHT_AUDITED` — *"there is no light-active pass to have been eligible for and skipped"*

`burpsy-go/internal/scanner/audit_engine.go:443` — *"lightAudit is the light-audit tier's per-run state (burpsy-react-ui-7bkj)"* — implements it, with the decision path at `:443-509`.

So the engine has a light tier, the parity table says it does not exist, and both live in `internal/scanner`. This is the third finding in this QA pass with the same shape: a bead closed on the mechanism, a stale claim left behind for the operator to read.

## Why it matters more than a stale comment

This table is the project's own **disclosure** of what it cannot do. Its whole purpose is to let a reader — or a reviewer comparing against Burp — see precisely which Burp behaviours are absent, so an absent capability is never discovered by surprise. A table that denies a capability the engine has is worse than no table: it makes every OTHER row in the table untrustworthy, because a reader who has just been wrong about light-auditing has no reason to believe the parameter-type or selection rows either.

## What the operator loses

- **Directly:** nothing yet — the engine is ahead of the disclosure.
- **Indirectly, and this is the real cost:** an operator reviewing the queue's parity panel concludes burpsy cannot do light audits and either does not configure them, or believes the light tier they selected is not happening. Both are wrong, and both change what they run against a live target.
- For a reviewer: `7bkj`'s close reason is contradicted by the file it claims to have completed.

## Fix

- Update the three rows against what the engine now does: `LIGHT_AUDITED` is reachable, `LIGHT_AUDITING` is a real transient, `NOT_LIGHT_AUDITED` is the repetitive-skip disposition. Each row's `Why` should name the actual behaviour, and a row that is now modelled belongs in the **modelled** list, not the not-modelled one.
- Then check every other row in the same table against the current engine — this pass found three stale rows in one table, which is enough to say the table was edited once and not re-audited.
- The audit-queue UI (`pages/auditqueue.tsx:79-119`) reduces the retained per-item evidence (Checks, Steps, Outcome, Breakers, point records, timestamps — all present in the API at `api_scanner_audit_items.go:133-150`) to six state totals, so even a corrected table has nothing to show. Burp's audit-item page exposes phase, requests, errors, insertion points scanned, and start/end time precisely so a partial audit can be diagnosed; the data is already retained, so surfacing it is a rendering change.
- A test that asserts the not-modelled list and the engine agree — for each row, that the named Burp status is genuinely unreachable. A stale row is then a failing test, not a comment someone has to re-read.

title: proxy: upstream TLS is never verified and has no policy — an invalid certificate is indistinguishable from a good one
description:
QA PASS 2026-09-25 — the proxy never verifies upstream TLS certificates, and offers no policy: no verify toggle, no custom CA, no protocol/cipher bounds.

## What is hardcoded

`burpsy-go/internal/proxy/tls_dial.go:95-100` — every intercepted TLS leg opens with `alpn.Dialer{InsecureSkipVerify: true, ...}`. The file's own comment explains why client certificates are configured there; it says nothing about verification, because verification is simply off. `internal/alpn/alpn.go:136-185` — the production TLS config — carries only `ServerName`, `InsecureSkipVerify`, `NextProtos` and the client-cert callback: no root pool, no `MinVersion`/`CipherSuites`, no renegotiation policy, no `ClientSessionCache` control, no SNI-off switch.

## What Burp offers (settings/network/tls.html:60-85, 138-155)

- verify upstream TLS (on by default, per **Burp**);
- select allowed protocols and cipher suites;
- allow unsafe renegotiation;
- disable session resumption;
- supply a custom CA;
- disable Java SNI for misconfigured servers;
- client certificates (burpsy HAS this one — `ClientCerts` is wired on the same dialer).

## Why this is filed as a P2 gap, not a security finding

A MITM proxy that verifies the upstream certificate would break the common case of an operator intercepting a site with a certificate burpsy's CA is not related to — but the certificate is still VALID, and a correctly chained one should verify. The current setting makes an invalid, expired, or hostname-mismatched upstream certificate indistinguishable from a good one: burpsy will proxy to a server presenting a certificate for a different name, and the operator sees a normal-looking exchange. That is a real fidelity loss for a tool whose job is to show what is really on the wire.

It is not filed as a security vulnerability because skipping verification on an interception leg is a recognized, deliberate MITM behavior and burpsy's own setting defaults to verifying. The gap is that burpsy has **no way to turn verification on**, and so cannot match Burp's default or reproduce a target that only presents a valid chain.

## The operator loses

- A target presenting an invalid, expired, self-signed-without-the-private-CA, or hostname-mismatched certificate: burpsy cannot detect or refuse it. An operator comparing two builds of the same app cannot tell from burpsy whether the certificate changed.
- Any policy requirement to constrain TLS versions or ciphers, or to forbid renegotiation.
- A private CA the target's issuer is not in the system pool, other than the certificate burpsy itself minted.

## Fix

- One setting, matching Burp's: verify upstream TLS, defaulting to ON. The interception leg then verifies against the system pool, with an escape hatch (a custom CA, or the existing "do not verify" switch) for the self-signed targets every assessor meets.
- Carry `MinVersion`/`CipherSuites` and a renegotiation policy through the same `alpn.Dialer` the sender already uses, so the proxy and the sender cannot drift.
- The custom-CA field is the same client-cert store shape burpsy already persists; one more entry in the network settings bundle.
close_reason: Every intercepted TLS leg opened with InsecureSkipVerify: true and nothing anywhere could turn it off, so an operator comparing two builds of the same app could not tell from burpsy whether the certificate had changed -- a swapped, expired, self-signed or hostname-mismatched certificate was indistinguishable from a good one. Verification now defaults to ON (Burp's default, and the only safe reading of a field whose absence would mean accept anything), with two escape hatches replacing the unconditional skip: a custom CA bundle that keeps verification on while trusting one more issuer, and verify:false as the deliberate opt-out for a self-signed lab target. Both live in NetworkSettings, so the setting is live, persisted and API-edited and the SAME edit reaches the sender and the proxy; the sender's TLSVerify is the fallback for a sender built without network settings applied. alpn.Dialer gained RootCAs and MinVersion, which is where the two legs would otherwise have drifted. A protocol floor below TLS 1.0 is refused rather than clamped, and a CA bundle that will not parse is reported when it is configured rather than at a later handshake. Eleven existing tests drive self-signed origins and began failing; that is the change working, and the fix was a named permissiveTLS() helper so each test declares it needs an unverified origin instead of relying on a skip that no longer exists. Verified live through a real console against a real self-signed origin: REFUSED with verification on, 200 after the operator's own CA was added with verification still on, 200 with verification explicitly off, each set through the console's API -- before the change the first case returned 200 silently. Mutation-checked three ways: restoring the hardcoded skip, dropping the custom CA from the dialer, and replacing the attached policy at restore. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./... green, tsc clean, bun test:lib 711/0, check:tokens green, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

title: network: redirects do not replay Set-Cookie, DNS has no address-family preference, and SOCKS cannot carry an upstream HTTP proxy
description:
QA PASS 2026-09-25 — three network settings Burp has that burpsy either lacks or applies too narrowly, filed together because each is one dial-path change in the sender or upstream package.

These are capability gaps with honest current behaviour. None of them is a lie on screen: the sender's open-ended declaration, the platform-auth setting's own help, and the upstream rule editor each say what they cover. What is missing is Burp's coverage, and in two cases the missing coverage is what makes a configured setting stop working on part of the traffic.

## 1. Followed redirects do not replay Set-Cookie (P2)

**Burp:** settings/tools/repeater.html:143-145 — *"If you enable this setting, Burp resubmits any cookies set in the redirect response when it follows the redirection target."*

**burpsy:** `internal/sender/redirect.go` builds each hop from the previous request only; `grep -n 'Set-Cookie'` finds one occurrence and it is a comment. `internal/web/repeater_options.go:18-22` states the absence plainly: redirect hops do not replay cookies.

**The operator loses:** login, SSO and consent flows that set a cookie during a redirect. The redirect is followed, the cookie is not sent, the destination returns the login page, and Repeater shows a page that looks like an application failure rather than a missing cookie. This is the single most common shape of a redirect in an authenticated tool.

**Fix:** ingest Set-Cookie from each hop's response into the jar the next hop is built from, and add the option Burp exposes so an operator can turn replay off for a target that sets throwaway cookies.

## 2. No DNS address-family preference (P2)

**Burp:** settings/network/dns.html:49-65 — system default, **Prefer IPv4**, or **Prefer IPv6**, *"because routing restrictions may permit only one family."*

**burpsy:** `internal/sender/network.go` offers system versus named-resolver selection plus exact hostname overrides, and returns the resolver's addresses unfiltered (`:485-518`). Address ordering is entirely the system resolver's.

**The operator loses:** any engagement on a host reachable only over one family. A dual-stack target behind IPv4-only routing can resolve to an AAAA first, and burpsy dials the unreachable address; the operator has no setting that fixes it and must override the hostname one address at a time.

**Fix:** a resolution-order option that filters or prefers an address family after the resolver answers, applied in the same place the existing hostname overrides are. It is a filter over an existing answer set, not a resolver rewrite.

## 3. SOCKS is a per-destination kind, not a global carrier (P2)

**Burp:** settings/network/connections.html:177-199 — SOCKS is a **global TCP layer**: *"every outbound connection, including requests to upstream HTTP proxies, goes through the SOCKS proxy"*, with per-host bypasses and a remote-DNS choice.

**burpsy:** `internal/web/api_network_proxy.go:15-21` makes proxy KIND part of each destination rule, and `internal/upstream/upstream.go` first-match selection returns exactly one proxy per destination. There is no layer beneath an HTTP upstream proxy.

**The operator loses:** the common corporate shape — burpsy reaches the internet through an HTTP proxy, and that HTTP proxy is itself only reachable through a SOCKS hop. With a single-layer rule the operator must choose one and lose the other. Global SOCKS bypasses are likewise inexpressible.

**Fix:** a global SOCKS carrier applied beneath whichever upstream proxy (or direct dial) a destination rule selects, with the same bypass list the destination rules use. The layering is a dial concern, so it belongs in `internal/upstream` rather than in the rule editor's model.

## Why these three together

Each is a small, well-understood change in code that already has the surrounding concept (the open-ended declaration, the hostname override table, the upstream policy). Filed together because they share a test surface — one target that redirects and sets a cookie, one dual-stack resolution, one nested proxy — and because they are the settings half of a gap the transport pass found alongside the two P1s already filed.
notes: Parts: 1) burpsy-react-ui-6wq7 (redirect cookie replay, done). 2) DNS address-family preference. 3) global SOCKS carrier beneath an upstream HTTP proxy. This bead stays open for 2 and 3.
close_reason: Burp's SOCKS setting is a global TCP layer (settings/network/connections.html:177-199): every outbound connection, including requests to upstream HTTP proxies, goes through the SOCKS proxy, with per-host bypasses and a remote-DNS choice. burpsy's model makes proxy KIND part of each destination rule and the policy returns exactly one proxy per address, so there was no layer beneath an HTTP upstream proxy -- an operator had to choose one and lose the other. The layering is a dial concern rather than a rule-editor one: a rule answers which proxy carries this host and a carrier answers what opens the socket to reach that proxy. A carrier carries a DIRECT destination (Burp says every connection), a proxied one, and a SOCKS-rule one, and exempts its own authority host AND port so the hop cannot dial itself; a host-only exemption made the layer silently do nothing for a dev-box operator, which the tests now pin. net.Dialer has no overridable dial field, so a dialer 'carrying' a carrier silently ignores it -- which is why the carrier is a dial FUNCTION applied at the one seam every connection opens through. A live pass found the routing bug the whole unit suite missed: every dial site read the carrier, the panel reported it configured, and the connection still went out direct, because Proxy.DialContext's KindDirect arm opened a bare net.Dialer and an operator who sets a SOCKS layer with no HTTP proxy has a policy resolving everything to Direct. One line in that arm is the feature, and TestADirectPolicyStillCarries is the regression that names it. The carrier is one instance shared by the sender, the proxy listener and the console, carried on SenderConfig at construction because the transport's client captures it then. An HTTPS upstream proxy is NOT carried -- crypto/tls has no dialer field to replace -- and the server reports that in the carrier's limits so the panel says 'Not carried' rather than the setting looking complete. Persisted beside the policy in its own settings row, restored FATAL on refusal. Verified live through a real console: with a carrier configured the SOCKS hop saw the connection and the origin saw none. Mutation-checked three ways plus the Direct arm. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./... green with the test cache cleared, tsc clean, bun test:lib 715/0, check:tokens green, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

title: intruder: Copy other payload is refused outside Pitchfork, which is the combination attack Burp documents it for
description:
QA PASS 2026-09-25 — Copy other payload is refused outside Pitchfork, which is the one combination attack Burp documents it for.

## What Burp's control is for

tools/intruder/configure-attack/payload-types.html:709-722 — *Copy other payload* copies the current payload to another position, and Burp gives the motivating case explicitly: two parameters that must always match, **with the Cluster bomb attack type used to manipulate the other parameters**. That is the entire reason a "copy another position" generator exists: hold two fields identical while the attack varies everything else.

## What burpsy does

- `burpsy-go/internal/web/api_tools.go:1007-1012` refuses every attack kind except pitchfork, with the message `copy_other: only supported in pitchfork, where every position advances in lockstep; <kind> does not guarantee the two positions match on every request`.
- `burpsy-go/internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx:2426-2432` labels the option Pitchfork-only in the UI, so the capability is visibly absent rather than broken.

## What the operator loses

The password / password-confirmation case, and every other "these two must match, vary the rest" shape. Pitchfork is a strict subset: it varies the copied pair TOGETHER, not the rest of the attack independently. A combination attack over a form whose confirmation field must track the password cannot be expressed.

## Already-tracked correction

`burpsy-react-ui-2g13` is CLOSED. Its reason is candid that copy_other is "refused outside pitchfork with a named reason (cluster bomb's mixed-radix Fill cannot guarantee the two positions match every request without a larger engine change)". The refusal is real and named, so nothing is misreported — but the bead's own title lists the payload type as delivered, and the documented use case is the one refused. This is the same class as the 03z parallel-send finding: a bounded, honest subset shipped under a bead that reads as full delivery.

## Fix

- Implement Copy other for cluster bomb: the copied positions are filled from their source's processed set by ordinal while the varied positions run their own mixed-radix enumeration, so the two tracks are independent.
- The engine change the close reason names is real but smaller than "larger engine": cluster bomb's Fill already walks a mixed-radix counter, so the copied positions need to consume their source set by the same counter value rather than being excluded from the enumeration.
- If that lands later, the option's help text should name the refused case rather than saying "Pitchfork only", so an operator knows what they are missing.
