title: settings.network: platform authentication supports only Basic and Digest — NTLMv1, NTLMv2 and Negotiate are absent, so NTLM/Kerberos-protected targets cannot be authenticated to
description:
## Burp-side evidence
Burp Settings → Network → Connections → Platform authentication supports schemes Basic, NTLMv1, NTLMv2, Negotiate and Digest (settings/network — "Platform authentication ... Type: Basic / NTLMv1 / NTLMv2 / Negotiate / Digest"). NTLM/Negotiate are needed for Windows-integrated and Kerberos-protected targets, a common enterprise case.

## burpsy-side evidence
internal/web/ui/src/pages/settings.network.tsx:106-107,119-129 offers only Basic and Digest and states outright that "NTLM needs the per-connection affinity the sender does not offer, and Negotiate needs a Kerberos credential rather than a password", so both are unavailable. A target behind NTLM/Negotiate cannot be authenticated to, and requests go out unauthenticated.

[DECISION] Adding NTLM/NTLMv2/Negotiate needs a sender/architecture change (per-connection auth affinity, Kerberos credential handling) — a product/architecture call.

comments.author: burpsy
comments.text: Claimed by the loop sweep, released: the issue is tagged decision-needed and the UI already states the architectural reason (NTLM needs per-connection affinity the sender does not offer; Negotiate needs a Kerberos credential). This is a sender-architecture call only the project owner can make, same class as kal/wkkz — not implementable without the decision. Released unchanged.

comments.author: burpsy
comments.text: PARTIAL — NTLMv2 only, landed in 3fb2ce1, NOT closing. What is real: the NTLMv2 crypto (NTOWFv2, LMv2 response, SessionBaseKey) and the NEGOTIATE/CHALLENGE/AUTHENTICATE codec, pinned to Microsoft's OWN published vectors from MS-NLMP rather than to self-consistency — TestNTLMv2TempMatchesTheSpecByteForByte and TestNTLMv2ResponseStartsWithTheNTProofStrMicrosoftPublished both pass, which is the right instrument when no domain controller is available in CI. Parsing refuses malformed input rather than inventing it (a target-info run past the end of the message; a challenge with no target info). Remaining and NOT done: NTLMv1, Negotiate/Kerberos, and — the important one — confirmation that this is WIRED into the platform-auth path end to end rather than being correct crypto nothing calls. That wiring check is the acceptance criterion for closing this bead; the vectors alone do not authenticate to anything.

comments.author: burpsy
comments.text: Verified 2026-09-16: the S5 unit's full work (uncommitted.patch, 757 lines + ntlmsession.go/ntlmsession_test.go in /root/handoff-20260916/S5-sel6/new/) applies CLEANLY to the merged HEAD, builds clean, and every patched package passes (netauth, sender, proxy, persist) after removing one unused 'time' import in ntlmsession_test.go. The patch contains the FULL platform-auth surface for NTLMv2: Domain/Workstation fields with refusal on non-NTLM rules, USER\DOMAIN username parsing with a conflict check, restore round-trip keeping domain (with the pre-migration empty-domain case preserved), SchemeNTLMv2 in ParseScheme with every NTLM spelling resolving to v2 and NTLMv1 refused as a downgrade with its crypto reason, SupportedSchemes carrying ntlmv2, UnsupportedScheme{Name,Reason} shipped to the panel, and the NTLMSession state machine (StartNTLM/NTLMChallengeHeader/Authenticate with its own 9 passing tests). NOT LANDED, and the reason is the acceptance criterion itself: 'correct crypto that nothing calls is not an authenticated request' — StartNTLM has ZERO call sites outside internal/netauth. The sender leg (the per-connection-affinity handshake the patch's own docstring calls sender.ntlmHandshake, which exists in no tree) is missing. Landing the panel-and-crypto half would create exactly the dead-option this repo refuses: an NTLMv2 selector that stores the credential, the panel reports it, and the requests still go out with a 401. The work stays preserved at /root/handoff-20260916/S5-sel6/ and is ready to build on when the sender leg is written. Remaining scope: internal/sender gains a per-exchange NTLM handshake (a connection cloned with MaxConnsPerHost=1, HTTP/2 off, three legs verified same-connection via httptrace, refusal on a bare-NTLM offer, per the S5 patch's own design notes in netauth.go's docstring).

title: session: no automatic macro parameter analysis / Re-analyze — every cross-step value wired by hand
description:
## Burp-side evidence
settings/sessions/macros.html — "When you define a new macro, Burp automatically tries to find any relationships ... identifying parameters whose values can be determined from the preceding response ... form field values, redirection targets, or query strings in links." plus a "Re-analyze macro" button and "Derive from prior response" parameter handling.

## burpsy-side evidence
pages/session.tsx requires every cross-step value to be declared by hand as an extraction (ExtractionRows, 228-331) and referenced as {{name}}. There is no automatic parameter-relationship analysis and no Re-analyze action; a CSRF token flow must be wired manually step by step.
close_reason: Shipped WHOLE, as the scoping comment required: analyzer + Re-analyze UI + apply flow as one unit. (1) session.AnalyzeMacro — a pure walk over a dry-run's responses finding the three classes Burp's own docs name, in confidence order: hidden form fields (the classic CSRF token; visible fields deliberately NOT suggested — their values are the operator's to type, not the response's to determine), Set-Cookie names, query strings in links. Skipped steps contribute nothing (no hallucination over a step that never ran); names the rule already extracts are not re-suggested (the list must not train the operator to ignore it); each suggestion carries the source and the value the response actually held so the relationship is checkable rather than magic. (2) POST /rules/{id}/analyze — Re-analyze, read-only, over the same dry-run /test runs. (3) POST /rules/{id}/apply-extractions — names only on the wire, the server rebuilds each extraction from its own current analysis (nothing client-shaped lands in the rule), stale name = 409 (the responses changed between look and commit; a silent no-op would let the UI claim a wiring that did not happen), Coordinator.AddExtraction is a single lock-held append refusing duplicates. (4) The rule editor: Re-analyze button beside Test macro, suggestion rows defaulting to picked, Wire N, and a baseline reset from the server after wiring so the next save cannot drop what was just wired. LIVE-VERIFIED end-to-end in one consistent run: the API drive (analyze found 3 with the origin's real values — csrf_token/sess/session from hidden-field/set-cookie/query-in-link; apply wired all three; dry-run resolved tok-FINAL-42/final-session-42/qFINAL42; rules API showed them on step 1; re-analyze after wiring honestly found 0; stale name 409) AND the UI drive (Re-analyze rendered three checkable rows, Wire 3 clicked, toast 'Wired 3 extractions', rule 3 carried all three server-side, Test-macro showed all three markers resolving). The honest-answer path was verified live too: when the fixture origin lapsed mid-drive, Re-analyze reported 'No new values' rather than inventing relationships. Tests: macro_analyze_test.go 6/6 (incl. the load-bearing every-pattern-lifts-its-value property), api_session_analyze_test.go 4/4. Gates: build/vet/gofmt clean, session+web suites green, tsc clean, bun test green, bundle rebuilt, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

comments.author: burpsy
comments.text: Claimed by the loop sweep, released after scoping: automatic parameter analysis is only useful shipped WHOLE — an analyzer endpoint without the Re-analyze UI and the apply-suggestions flow would be a capability an operator cannot reach, which this repo's rules treat as a defect rather than progress. The implementation shape (server analyzer over a dry-run's responses: form fields with values, hidden inputs, Set-Cookie names, query strings in links → suggested Extractions with {{name}} wiring into later steps; UI: Re-analyze button + suggestion list + apply) is recorded here for the session-epic owner (a09g) to take as one unit.

title: session: cookie jar shows only host/name/value — no path, domain, expiry or Secure/HttpOnly
description:
## Burp-side evidence
settings/sessions/index.html — "The cookie jar honors the domain and path scope of cookies." Burp's cookie jar viewer shows domain/path and lets you edit each cookie's attributes.

## burpsy-side evidence
pages/session.tsx:1025-1040 renders the jar as three columns only: Authority (host+scheme), Name, Value. There is no Path, Domain, Expiry, or Secure/HttpOnly column, so two cookies differing only by path are indistinguishable and scope attributes are invisible.
close_reason: Storage first, columns second, because columns over a jar that ignores its own attributes would document a policy the engine does not have. RFC 6265 modelled: absorb keeps §5.3 attributes (Path/Domain/Expires/Max-Age/Secure/HttpOnly, unmodelled ones skipped by name), storage key becomes (domain, path, name) so two cookies differing only by path coexist, and CookieHeader(host, port, tls, path) enforces all four §5.4 rules at send time: domain-match against the REQUEST host (cross-jar scan — a Domain=.app.test cookie set at app.test serves sub.app.test; the authority split groups the table, it is not a §5.4 boundary), path-match, expiry, Secure-judged-by-request-TLS. Host-only cookies stay bound to the exact setting authority (port+TLS). Every caller threads the request's real path: proxy relay, crawler gate+macros, Repeater/Intruder, login probe, scanner auth contexts, CLI. Session table gains a Scoping column fed by the same attributes the jar enforces; wire type gains the same optional fields. Verified: jar_attrs_test.go 9 tests stating §5.3/§5.4 facts (attributes survive absorb; path-scoped cookie not sent elsewhere; two same-name path-differing cookies coexist; domain covers subdomains, host-only does not; Max-Age=0 expires; Secure refused over plaintext for host-only AND domain cookies; remove deletes every path instance; operator-set cookie still sent everywhere). Mutation checks observed: pathMatches->always-true FAILs both path tests; subdomain drop FAILs the domain test; Secure drop originally PASSED (authority check shielded it) so the domain-Secure test was added and now FAILs under the same mutation; expiry mutation is unkillable compile-error (orphans now) — expected survivor, noted. Gates: go build/vet/gofmt clean; go test session/web/proxy/crawler/sender/scanner/cmd all ok (scanner under its own 1800s timeout — first run's FAIL was the 600s default deadline); e2e-go.sh 24/24; tsc clean; bun test pass; dist/app.js rebuilt. Committed 3991495.

comments.author: burpsy
comments.text:
Scoping note before anyone implements this as a column change — it is not one.

internal/session/session.go:725-729 states the jar's current contract explicitly: 'Attributes are dropped rather than modelled: nothing in this port acts on Path, Domain or Expires yet, and a jar that stored them would imply a scoping and expiry policy it does not enforce.'

So adding Path/Domain/Expiry/Secure columns to pages/session.tsx on their own would display scope attributes while the jar keeps sending every cookie to every path on the authority regardless of them. That is worse than the current gap: an operator reading 'Path=/admin' would reasonably conclude the cookie is not being sent to /login, and it is.

The issue title is right that two cookies differing only by path are indistinguishable — but the reason is that the jar cannot HOLD two such cookies at all. cookieJar.m is map[name]value keyed on the name alone, so the second Set-Cookie overwrites the first. There is nothing to display.

The real shape, which also closes the honest version of this issue:

1. jarCookie{Name, Value, Path, Domain string; Expires time.Time; Secure, HttpOnly bool}, keyed by (domain, path, name) per RFC 6265 §5.3.
2. absorb parses and keeps the attributes instead of cutting at the first semicolon.
3. cookieHeader gains a path (and keeps the tls flag it has) and does RFC 6265 §5.4 domain-match, path-match, Secure-only-over-TLS and expiry filtering.
4. Then the columns, which are now reporting something that is true.

Step 3 changes CookieHeader(host, port, tls) -> needs a path, which ripples to six call sites plus the CookieHeader interface in internal/crawler/session_gate.go:72: api_tools.go:357, api_session.go:849, session/recovery.go:300 and the crawler gate.

Bounded, but a jar-semantics change rather than a UI change, and it overlaps burpsy-react-ui-dkb (the jar is read-only) — whoever takes one should look at both. Releasing my claim so it is picked up with this scope in view rather than as a four-column patch.

title: session: rules have no parameter scope — cannot restrict a rule to requests carrying a named parameter
description:
## Burp-side evidence
settings/sessions/session-handling-rules.html — "Parameter scope. You can specify that rules should only apply to requests containing specific named parameters. This enables you to create a rule that updates a certain parameter across all requests, such as a CSRF token."

## burpsy-side evidence
pages/session.tsx rule editor has Name, Enabled, Max attempts, Hosts, Validity, Steps — no parameter-scope field. SessionRuleFull (lib/types.policy.ts) has no parameter-scope member, so a rule cannot be restricted to requests carrying a named parameter.
close_reason: SessionRule.ScopeParams + MatchParams (every named parameter present, case-insensitive — csrf_token vs CSRF_Token is the same parameter; empty = unrestricted, matching MatchHost's empty-list contract so legacy rules cannot silently stop matching). MatchingRuleFor(host, params) is the evaluating entry point; MatchingRule stays parameter-less so callers that could pass params but don't are visible in grep. Login probe passes its steps' parameter names (URL query + form-urlencoded body — Burp's two scope surfaces; JSON has no names without a schema). Axis is a restriction, not a priority: scoped-first claims its requests and falls through everything else. Persisted as session_rules.scope_params (JSON list, DEFAULT '' via addColumn — legacy reads unrestricted, the only safe default). UI: scope_params on the rule DTO both directions (omitted=everywhere), editor gains the parameter list mirroring the host list, summary reads 'every host carrying csrf_token'. title: session: cookie-jar monitored-tool set is hardcoded to Proxy — cannot monitor Repeater/Intruder/Scanner/etc

close_reason: Shipped in the honest order the scoping comment demanded — surfaces first, then the toggle. SURFACES: the Repeater absorbs in recordRepeaterExchange (raw bytes, after the store write, attributed SourceRepeater); the Intruder absorbs in its RecordFn where the engine stores one exemplar per result bucket (the jar sees each distinct behaviour's Set-Cookie, the same memory contract the engine holds); the scanner absorbs in sendTestRequestFull at the one place every probe response passes (not decoration — the audit's auth-diff consumes the jar, so a rotating-session audit keeps its authenticated context only because this exists); the proxy keeps its absorb now attributed SourceProxy; the web layer attaches its three at WithSessionCoordinator, the same registered-when-wired rule WithCookieJar holds. TOGGLE: Coordinator.SetMonitoredSources/MonitoredSources; AbsorbResponseCookies widens to carry the source; a switched-off source's response COUNTS as observed and absorbs nothing — attached-but-off must not render as vanished, the three-state honesty the observation counters exist for. Default every source on, matching the contract note AbsorbResponseCookies has carried since proxy-only: a disabled-by-default entry would silently un-fill a jar that was filling. Empty list refused at the route (400) and guarded in the UI (never below one). POST /api/session/cookies {action:monitor,tools} configures; GET reports monitored beside absorbing_from; the Session jar card renders one checkbox per attached source from that pair. LIVE-VERIFIED: a Repeater send through the real API deposited its cookie in the jar; the toggle through the API switched the Repeater off and the counters read responses_observed=4 set_cookies_absorbed=3 — the three-state contract MEASURED, not asserted; the UI rendered the four toggles truthfully, 'Now monitoring 3 tools' on enable, and 'At least one tool must be monitored — the jar would never fill' refusing the last un-tick. Mutations: monitors-check inverted FAILs both tests; observation-gated-on-monitoring FAILs; empty-set-honoured is an equivalent at the session layer (the route 400 is the real defense, pinned by its own test). Tests: monitored_test.go 4/4, session_monitored_tools_test.go 4/4, existing absorb suite on the new signature. Gates: build/vet/gofmt clean, session+web+proxy green, tsc clean, bun test green, bundle rebuilt, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

comments.author: burpsy
comments.text: Claimed by the loop sweep, released after scoping. The monitored-tool set is a toggle over absorbing SURFACES, and today there is exactly one (the proxy) — Repeater/Intruder/Scanner never call AbsorbResponseCookies, so a configurable set would be a control wired to nothing (this repo ships those deliberately never). Honest sequencing: first each surface gains absorption at its capture point (Repeater's sendGroup/store write, Intruder's per-attempt response, the scanner's audit reads), recording per-source counters via AttachAbsorptionSource which ALREADY reports per-surface observation; THEN this toggle defaults-on for all absorbing surfaces and is meaningful. The toggle must default on per absorb.go's own contract note. Sequencing recorded here for the session epic (a09g) owner.

title: session: rules cannot be reordered, so precedence between overlapping rules is uncontrollable
description:
## Burp-side evidence
settings/sessions/index.html: "By creating multiple rules, you can define a hierarchy of behavior... Every time Burp makes an outgoing request, it determines which of the defined rules should apply... and then performs all of the relevant actions in order." Macros: "You can also edit your existing macros, or change their position in the list."

## burpsy-side evidence
session.tsx rule list (650-696) renders each rule with only Enable/Edit/Delete; there are no move-up/move-down controls (contrast StepCard 372-382, which does have them for macro steps). SectionHeading (633-635) states "the first that applies owns the recovery" — so order is significant — yet a rule's position cannot be changed, so precedence between two overlapping rules cannot be controlled without deleting and recreating.
close_reason:
Implemented end to end: session rules can now be reordered, so precedence between overlapping rules is controllable.

Backend — Coordinator.MoveRule(id, offset) (internal/session/session.go, next to AllRules): moves a rule within the evaluation order slice by a signed offset, returns the new position. Design points, all documented in the code: (1) Moving is the ONLY way precedence could change and it is deliberately separate from UpdateRule, which 'keeps its identity (ID and position in the evaluation order)' — the old workaround, delete + re-add, minted a fresh id and broke every saved /api/session/rules/{id}/run reference while silently inverting precedence. (2) Signed offset rather than absolute index: a concurrent AddRule/RemoveRule between the operator loading the table and clicking shifts the rule relative to its neighbours instead of swapping it with whatever now sits at the target index. (3) Refusals, not clamps: a move past either end returns the new sentinel ErrRuleAtEdge (400 naming the edge) instead of a silent success that changed nothing; unknown id is ErrNoSuchRule (404). offset 0 is a no-op read reporting the current position. MatchingRule walks the same order slice, so the moved rule's precedence takes effect immediately and the id is never renumbered.

API — POST /api/session/rules/{id}/move with {"offset": -1|+1|N} (internal/web/api_session.go: sessionRuleMove, dispatched in handleSessionRuleDetail alongside the existing /update-macro and /run suffix routes). Answers {"position": N}; 404 unknown rule; 400 edge-refusal with the edge named; 405 with Allow: POST for other methods. Order is persisted immediately via persistSessionRules(), so a restart restores the moved rule at its new position (the restore path calls RestoreRule in persisted order — precedence survives restarts).

UI — session.tsx: up/down ArrowUp/ArrowDown IconButtons on each rule row (edge-disabled), calling new hook useMoveSessionRule (data.policy.ts) which POSTs the move and invalidates the session query so the table always shows the live evaluation order. New useMoveSessionRule hook documented with the 400/404 contract.

Tests — 11 new, all full-sentence claims per package convention:
internal/session/move_test.go (6): move swaps adjacent rules and MatchingRule hands the host to the moved rule; down-move updates position (second,first,third order asserted); moves past either edge are refused NOT clamped and refused moves change nothing; unknown id = ErrNoSuchRule; offset 0 is a positional read; the id is stable across the move (the delete+re-add hazard).
internal/web/session_move_api_test.go (5): wire round trip flips matcher ownership (allow_all scopes make position the only decider); unknown rule 404; past-the-top 400 whose body names the edge; GET on /move 405 with Allow: POST; persisted order after the move starts with the moved rule (AllRules is what SaveSessionRules writes).

Gate — go build ./... clean; go vet ./... clean; gofmt -l . empty; go test ./... all ok (including 167 UI checks via bun run check, 0 fail); UI bundle rebuilt (bun run build) since it is go:embed-ed. e2e: QUICK=1 e2e-go.sh = 20 passed / 4 failed, IDENTICAL on the clean HEAD baseline via git stash — the 4 failures (history path/status capture) pre-exist on this branch and are unrelated to session rules; no regression from this change.

title: intruder: no redirection handling — the attack never follows a 3xx and there is no Follow-redirections setting, so a result only visible after a redirect is missed
description:
## Burp-side evidence
tools/intruder/configure-attack/settings.html (Redirections) — Intruder attack settings include "Follow redirections" (Never / On-site only / In-scope only / Always) and "Process cookies in redirections", so an attack can chase a 3xx to the page that actually carries the result.

## burpsy-side evidence
internal/intruder/intruder.go:27-31 states the engine "does not follow redirects at all" and that the redirect config field was deliberately removed. internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx exposes no redirect setting. A login/brute-force attack whose success is only observable after a 302 sees only the 302.

[DECISION] burpsy removed redirect-following on purpose for scope-safety (per-hop re-authorisation through the scope chokepoint). Reaching Burp parity needs a product/architecture call on whether to reintroduce scoped redirect-following.
close_reason: Follow redirections wired via sender.AuthorisedSender.FollowRedirectsAfterPolicy inside the intruder send closure, re-authorising each hop through scope exactly as Repeater's own redirect override does (internal/web/api_tools.go, commit 3a275b3). follow_redirects wire field + redirects_followed report counter; UI select + metric tile (commit bca62a0). Verified over real sockets: unset leaves the 302 as the response and the follow-target unhit; always reaches the final page and counts the hop; an out-of-scope hop is refused and the follow-target is never contacted. Revert-and-rerun confirmed the positive test fails without the fix. Full non-intruder Go suite and frontend gate clean.

title: intruder: no 'URL-encode these characters' payload encoding — the default final-pass character encoding of the Payloads panel is absent, only a whole-payload encode processing rule exists
description:

Encoding is reachable only as an ordered processing rule (PAYLOAD_RULES "encode" with a layer, types.tools.ts:30, intruder.tsx:1274-1304), which URL-encodes the entire payload rather than a chosen character set and does not run as an automatic final pass. The default "URL-encode these characters" safety net is absent.
close_reason: intruder.URLEncodeSet(ps, chars): the final pass — named characters percent-encoded per UTF-8 byte, everything else untouched (the whole-payload encode rule remains the separate tool); spaces and control characters always encoded additionally (a payload containing them cannot be delivered); empty named set with nothing unrepresentable is the off state. Applied in handleIntruderRun AFTER the operator's rule chain (Burp's placement) — the two compose. Wire: url_encode_characters on /api/intruder/run. UI: the box under Payload processing, seeded with Burp's default list, clearable to disable. Tests: TestURLEncodeSet* (5, incl. multi-byte per-byte and the always-encode rule), TestIntruderRunAppliesURLEncodeCharacters (wire, x y -> x%20y in the echo). Commits d93be4f + 2847ca9.

## burpsy-side evidence

There is no honest smaller shape — a custom column without operator-defined code is a fixed column, and inventing a burpsy-only scripting runtime would contradict the design decision recorded the same week. The shipped surfaces that serve the underlying need (visible per-row operator knowledge) are live: annotation fields (notes + highlight, editable from the history table) and the task field in the filter grammar (6n4d). The parity audit already classified the extension model 'by design, not a gap'; this is that same boundary applied to one UI surface.

JSON-RPC plugin registrations of kind custom-column? a restricted expression DSL like the history filter's?). Recorded here so the next sweep does not re-derive it.

comments.author: burpsy
comments.text: PRODUCT DECISION RECORDED 2026-09-20, per the operator's standing directive: Burp's custom columns are Bambda/Montoya SCRIPT-defined columns — they require exactly the JVM/Java scripting model this project documents as a deliberate non-goal (host.go:339-343, extension/AGENTS.md:9-13, and wkkz just closed as wontfix-by-design on the same basis). There is no honest smaller shape: a 'custom column' without operator-defined code is a fixed column, and inventing a burpsy-only scripting runtime would contradict the recorded non-goal the same week it was made. The shipped alternative that serves the underlying need (visible per-row operator knowledge): the annotation fields (notes + highlight) plus the task field in the filter grammar, both live. Closing as wontfix-by-design, same class as wkkz.

title: history: no Listener port column — multiple listeners are indistinguishable in history

title: sequencer: no 'ignore tokens whose length deviates by X characters' capture filter
description:
## Burp-side evidence
settings/tools/sequencer.html — Live capture: "Ignore token whose length deviates by X characters - Enable this setting to ignore tokens that deviate by a specified number of characters from the average token length. This setting is useful if the application occasionally returns a different item in the location where a token normally appears."

## burpsy-side evidence
No length-deviation filter exists. burpsy-go/internal/web/api_sequencer_capture.go keeps every extracted string as a token (missCount only records extraction failures, not length outliers); pages/sequencer.tsx has no such setting. A stray wrong-length item in the token location silently pollutes the sample instead of being dropped.
close_reason: Implemented. length_deviates {enable, chars} on the capture request; the worker drops tokens whose length deviates from the RUNNING average (maintained as a sum under the capture mutex — first token never filtered, no sample copy) by more than chars, counting each drop as a miss with its reason while resetting the miss streak like a hit. UI gains the 'Ignore length deviates ±' input, empty = off. TestLengthDeviationFilterDropsOutliersAndCountsThem pins both halves against an origin alternating token lengths; mutation disabling the filter failed with three 'survived' lines and 'misses = 0' (observed), restored green. Full web suite ok, tsc clean, dist rebuilt.

title: sequencer: live capture has no thread/concurrency control — only a per-request delay
description:
## Burp-side evidence
settings/tools/sequencer.html — Live capture settings: "Number of threads - Specify the maximum number of concurrent requests that the live capture can make." Burp captures tokens with a configurable concurrency pool.

## burpsy-side evidence
burpsy-go/internal/web/api_sequencer_capture.go:354-358 — the capture request struct exposes only `Count` and `DelayMs`; the capture loop is single-threaded and paced only by delay. There is no thread/concurrency control, so a 5000-token capture over a slow app cannot be parallelised. pages/sequencer.tsx:480-502 exposes only "Requests" and "Delay (ms)" fields.
close_reason: Live capture becomes a worker pool: threads (default 1 = the historical sequential capture, cap 32, refused beyond rather than clamped). Claims CAS-issued from an atomic counter — claims are promises to send, attempts are settled sends; the sequential loop's attempt()<requested check was safe only because one goroutine ran it. Both pauses gate between sends in every worker (same placement as before, so a pause never splits a response). Miss-streak guard: per-worker streak, so a location that never matches stops in the same order of magnitude of requests the sequential guard produced (a global streak ÷ thread count would have cost threads×25 requests on a broken location). Cancellation classifies in the closer — several workers see ctx.Done at once and exactly one task.Stop lands, so the dashboard reads a cancelled capture as stopped. Wire: threads on the capture request; form gains the field with the shared-bound caveat in the hint. Tests: threads=1 never overlaps, threads=4 overlaps and collects every token, threads=33 refused, wide pool never claims one ordinal twice (origin stamps tokens at ACCEPT time — stamping at write time races across overlapping connections and mimics the duplicate-claim defect). Verified live through the UI: three 100-token captures completed. Commit c36ce21.

title: repeater: no WebSocket messages in Repeater — a frame cannot be sent, edited (to server or client) and resent; Repeater is HTTP-only
description:
Burp Repeater is not HTTP-only: a WebSocket message can be sent to Repeater, edited, and resent
against the live connection, with a choice of sending to server or client. burpsy's Repeater is
HTTP-only. WebSocket traffic is visible in Proxy > WebSockets history but is read-only there
(`burpsy-react-ui-nmv`: the frame table has no context menu, so a frame cannot even be sent
anywhere), and Repeater has no WebSocket tab type.

## Burp-side evidence

`/root/burp-re/in/extract/resources/Documentation/burp/documentation/desktop/tools/repeater/websocket-messages.html`:

> You can use Burp Repeater to manipulate and resend individual WebSocket messages... Right-click on
> a WebSocket message, and click **Send to Repeater**... Modify the message. Select whether the
> message should be sent to the server or client. Click **Send**... To resend the message,
> right-click on it and click **Edit and resend**.

> For WebSocket messages, each Repeater tab contains ... A message editor ... The WebSocket
> connection via which the message is sent. This is set automatically when you send a message [from
> WebSockets history].

`managing-tabs.html` confirms the tab type is first-class: "Burp Repeater opens each new HTTP or
WebSocket message in a new tab ... click the button. Select either **HTTP** or **WebSocket**."

## burpsy-side evidence

- `internal/web/ui/src/pages/repeater.tsx` — `RepeaterTab` carries `target`/`request`/`protocol`
  (http/https) only; the editor and send path assume an HTTP request/response. There is no WebSocket
  tab, no direction (to-server / to-client) control, and no held-connection concept.
- `internal/web/ui/src/pages/wshistory.tsx` is read-only (see `burpsy-react-ui-nmv`), so there is no
  "Send to Repeater" origin for a frame either.

## Decision

This is a subsystem, not a control: it needs a persistent client-side WebSocket the operator can
frame against (server *and* client direction), a new Repeater tab type, and a "Send to Repeater"
path out of WebSockets history. Sizing and whether to build it is a product decision, hence the
[DECISION] marker. Blocks nothing else; blocked by the wshistory frame menu (`nmv`) for the
natural entry point.
notes: DECISION 2026-09-23 (Main, per the session goal to finish all open issues): build it. Scope = one-shot send against a fresh WebSocket dial per resend, not a held live connection. Rationale: burpsy's Repeater has no held-socket concept today and the proxy's intercept is a hold, not a session; a persistent client-side connection pool is a subsystem whose failure modes (socket lifetime, reconnect, target-side limits) would swallow the deliverable. The bead's contract is send/edit/resent with a direction choice; a one-shot dial satisfies all three, and the honest note in the UI says the frame goes out on a NEW connection, which Burp does too for its 'set automatically' when the original has closed. The direction choice's to-client half: burpsy cannot inject into a third party's client socket on a fresh dial, so to-client is offered only when a live intercepted connection is holding that frame's connection - the same hold the proxy already implements. For one-shot sends, to-server is the path; to-client without a live socket is refused with the reason shown, not hidden.
close_reason: One-shot resend over a fresh dial, as the bead's recorded decision scoped it (a held client-side socket pool is a subsystem whose failure modes would swallow the deliverable; the send/edit/resend + direction contract is satisfied by a fresh dial, which is also Burp's behaviour once the original has closed). internal/sender gains SendUpgrade (one dial through the existing resolution + upstream-proxy path, operator's upgrade bytes verbatim, live socket returned only on a 101, ALPN HTTP/1.1 only); internal/wsclient owns the one-shot send and reuses core's frame codec and WsReassembler so a frame is encoded by the same rules history's rows are decoded by. Direction: to-server runs; to-client is answered 400 with its reason BEFORE any dial (a refusal that has already opened a socket has sent traffic the operator did not choose) and names the proxy's intercept hold as the surface that can do it. Scope is not bypassable by framing: the host gate at prepare plus AuthoriseRaw on the handshake bytes. The resend is recorded as its own conversation - the real 101 exchange plus both frames as WsMessages - so it sits in WebSockets history beside the original. UI: a first-class Repeater tab type (kind ws, wsPayload/wsOpcode on the store) plus a 'Send to Repeater' action on a wshistory frame. The orphaned WIP carried five defects, all fixed: the route was never registered (every test 404'd); to-client dialled the target before refusing; the echo target's frame reader dereferenced a nil header, because core.ParseWsFrameHeader answers (nil, needMore, nil) when it wants more bytes and a masked frame needs 6 before its length is knowable; the scope test excluded 'host:port' as a pattern, which matches no host (scope rules carry host/path/port as separate fields) so the gate passed for the wrong reason; and the frame assertions read the store's newest-first order as chronological. Verified live against a hand-rolled RFC 6455 target with a real Sec-WebSocket-Accept: frame out, 'echo: hello from burpsy' back, peer closed 1000, and the conversation readable in /api/ws/history with the two direction filters splitting it 1/1. tsc clean, bun test 676/0, go vet/gofmt/build clean, web+sender+proxy green. NOT live-verified: the Repeater WS pane's rendered UI (browser host down this session). Commit f2862e0.

comments.author: burpsy
comments.text: Claimed by the loop sweep, released after scoping: a WebSocket Repeater is a new tab TYPE, not a Repeater extension. It needs (1) a live-connection manager — connect, hold open across sends, show interleaved replies, close — which no current surface has (the proxy's WS relay forwards; it does not hold an origin connection open for interactive use), (2) a frame-shaped send endpoint (SendFrameProgram exists for h2 programs but nothing equivalent carries an outbound WS frame to an origin with scope checks), (3) direction control (to-server vs to-client — the client side needs a burpsy-hosted WS endpoint the target's page connects to, which is its own service), and (4) RepeaterTab model + UI for all of it. Multi-day epic-sized work; belongs planned under the cross-tool shell (srzn) with its own design pass rather than built half-way here. The read-only gap it compounds (no context menu on WS history frames) is nmv.

title: sequencer: token location is free-text only, with no picker over the response and no form-field option
description:
## Claim
The Sequencer's token location is typed as free text with no dropdown of what the response actually contains, and Burp's "Form field" location has no counterpart.

## Burp-side evidence
`tools/sequencer/sample/index.html`, "Selecting a token location" — all three are pickers over the response, not free text:
> "You can specify the token you want to analyze in the Token location within response panel. The following options are available:
> **Cookie** - Select a cookie from the drop-down list. This is the most common method to pass session tokens to clients.
> **Form field** - Select an HTML form field value from the drop-down list. You can use this method to transmit anti-CSRF tokens and other per-page tokens to clients.
> **Custom location** - Specify a custom location within the response that contains the token you want to analyze. This uses the response extraction rule dialog."

`getting-started.html` step 5: "Select a cookie in the Token location within response panel."

`BURP_SUITE_UI_UX_SPECIFICATION.md` §4.8: "Token Location selector (Cookie name, Form field, Custom regex match)."

## burpsy-side evidence
Three kinds, all typed by hand — `internal/web/ui/src/pages/sequencer.tsx:448-479`:
```tsx
<option value="cookie">Set-Cookie value</option>
<option value="header">Response header value</option>
<option value="body_regex">Body, by pattern</option>
```
followed by a free-text `Input` for the cookie name / header name (`:469-478`) or the RE2 pattern (`:458-467`). No option is populated from a response.

Server side, `tokenLocation` (`internal/web/api_sequencer_capture.go:56-58`) matches those three kinds and compiles the pattern (`:87`). There is no form-field extractor:
- `cookie` reads a Set-Cookie value
- `header` reads a response header value
- `body_regex` applies an RE2 pattern

A form field is reachable *only* by the operator hand-writing a regex for it, which is a different task from picking a name off a list — and the regex has to be right about the surrounding HTML.

## The deliberate part, and where it stops
Declared-not-guessed is an explicit design choice and is disclosed — `internal/web/ui/src/pages/sequencer.tsx:422-425`:
> "The token location is declared, not guessed: a heuristic that picked the wrong cookie would produce a confident verdict about the wrong string."

That reasoning defends refusing to *auto-select* a location. It does not defend refusing to *offer* the list: presenting the cookies and form fields actually present in a captured response, for the operator to choose from, is still a declaration — the operator picks. So the disclosure covers auto-detection, not the absence of a picker, and this issue is scoped to the picker.

This depends on the send-to-Sequencer issue: a picker needs a response to populate from, which the paste-a-raw-request flow does not have.

## Classification
CAPABILITY GAP (form-field location; picker) — not covered by the existing disclosure.

## What an operator cannot do
Pick the token. They must already know the exact cookie or header name before opening the page, and for an anti-CSRF form token they must write a working regex against HTML they cannot see on this page.
acceptance_criteria: When a request arrives with a response (via send-to-Sequencer), the token location offers the cookies, headers and HTML form fields actually present in that response as selectable options, plus a form-field extractor server-side. The operator still chooses — nothing is auto-selected — so the declared-not-guessed disclosure stays true.
close_reason: Token location picker + form-field extractor. Hand-off half: Send to Sequencer (fhp) now carries the response, and the capture form parses it client-side into cookies/headers/form-fields actually present (sequencer-token-options.ts, own tests) — names + value excerpts; nothing auto-selected (placeholder names the count and asks the operator to pick), typed input remains when no response arrived, and the hint names which state you are in — the declared-not-guessed disclosure stays true. Server half: tokenLocation gains form_field — parsed, not regexed: value of an input/select/textarea by name, case-insensitive attrs and name, double/single-quoted values read, empty value and absent field refused naming the field; compile requires a name; joins cookie/header in every refusal path and Describe. Verified: parser tests pin all three lists against a mixed response + empty-body case; extractor test pins quote shapes, case-insensitivity, both refusals; full web suite green; 302 lib tests; tsc; dist; sequencer route + axe 0 both themes.

title: organizer: cannot show a saved exchange's request and response — only a jump to HTTP history
description:
## Claim
The Organizer cannot show a saved exchange's request and response — selecting a row offers only a jump to HTTP history.

## Burp-side evidence
`tools/organizer/index.html`, "Inspecting a message in Organizer":
> "Select a message to inspect its request and response in the lower pane. Both are shown as read-only snapshots.
> To search within the request or response, use the search bar below the message.
> Use the tabs beside the message to switch between the Inspector and Notes panels."

And the snapshot semantics, stated earlier on the same page: "Messages appear in the Organizer inbox as **read-only copies** of the original request and response, including any notes and highlights."

## burpsy-side evidence
The detail card renders the note editor only — `internal/web/ui/src/pages/organizer.tsx:450-533`: Title, Highlight swatches, and an "Investigation note" textarea. No message editor.

Viewing the bytes means leaving the page — `internal/web/ui/src/pages/organizer.tsx:233-237`:
```ts
/** Reveal the underlying exchange in HTTP history rather than copying its bytes here. */
const openInHistory = (exchange: number) => {
  focusExchange(exchange);
  setRoute("history");
};
```
reached from a per-row icon button (`:422-431`) and a "Show in history" action (`:459-462`).

## The design tension worth deciding
burpsy stores a *reference*, not a copy: `organizer.Item` holds `Exchange int` (`internal/organizer/organizer.go:10`), and the page states the intent — `pages/organizer.tsx:455`: "The note stays attached to the exchange, not to a copy of its bytes."

That choice is defensible and has a visible consequence the page handles well: when the exchange is evicted, the row shows "exchange no longer retained" (`pages/organizer.tsx:402-408`) and is exempted from filters with a stated reason (`pages/organizer.tsx:20-37`).

But it is also the reason the bytes cannot be shown reliably, and it diverges from Burp, where the copy is the point — the item survives independently of history. So:

1. Add a read-only request/response pane resolving from the traffic store on demand. Cheapest; inherits the unresolved state that already exists. An evicted exchange still cannot be inspected.
2. Store a byte snapshot at save time, matching Burp. Removes the unresolved-row state entirely, at a memory cost, and makes the Organizer usable as evidence after eviction — which is what an operator saving something for a report actually wants.

(2) is the larger change and the better match to what the tool is for; (1) is a real improvement available now. Worth an explicit decision rather than defaulting to (1) because it is easier.

## Classification
CAPABILITY GAP.

## What an operator cannot do
Read what they saved, in the place they saved it. Every look at a shortlisted exchange is a round trip to HTTP history and back, and once the exchange is evicted the note survives with no way to see what it was about.
acceptance_criteria: Selecting an Organizer item shows its request and response read-only on the Organizer page. Whether bytes are snapshotted at save time or resolved from the traffic store is decided and recorded; if resolved, an evicted exchange keeps the existing explicit unresolved state.
close_reason: Added a read-only request/response pane to the Organizer detail card, resolved on demand from the traffic store (not a byte snapshot at save time — decision recorded in code comments per the bead's acceptance criteria) through the same message-store ids and useMessage/HttpEditor History already uses. api_organizer_view.go's organizerItemView gained Request/Response *uint64 fields (pointers so message id 0 is not dropped by omitempty). Verified: new Go tests in api_organizer_view_test.go (request/response ids on the wire, id-0 not dropped, absent when unresolved), a new e2e spec (organizer-message-pane.spec.ts, 1 passed) that saves a real seeded exchange and reads its actual bytes back off the Organizer page, and the full tsc/bun test/bun build + go build/test gate. Revert-and-fail confirmed on both the Go and e2e side (see commit message).

title: organizer and logger: neither can export as CSV, though HTTP history can
description:
## Claim
Neither the Organizer nor the Logger can export as CSV, though HTTP history can.

## Burp-side evidence
`tools/organizer/index.html`, "Exporting results":
> "You can export Organizer items as a CSV file to easily share with others or include in your reports. […] To export all items: Right-click the table then select **Export as CSV**. […] To export specific items: Select the items that you want to export. Right-click and select Export as CSV."

`tools/logger/entries.html`, "Export log entries as CSV":
> "To export log entries as a CSV file, select the relevant entries in the table, right-click and select **Export as CSV**. The whole table is exported if you select zero entries or one entry."

Both docs specify escaping in detail — comma wrapping, doubled quotes, and an Excel guard: "Any data starting with -, +, = or @ is escaped for Excel by prefixing a single quote (')".

## burpsy-side evidence
Exactly one CSV path exists in the UI, and it is History's:
```
$ grep -rn "csv\|CSV" internal/web/ui/src --include=*.tsx --include=*.ts
internal/web/ui/src/lib/api.ts:121,123,157,164,173,180,197,209,210   (historyToCSV and helpers)
internal/web/ui/src/pages/history.tsx:6,594-605,877-879             (exportCSV + the button)
internal/web/ui/src/app.tsx:26,179                                  (desktop shell File > Export History)
```
`lib/api.ts:157` documents it as "The one CSV shape in the app: the History…". No hit under `pages/organizer.tsx` or `pages/logger.tsx`.

Confirmed against the pages themselves: the Organizer's header actions are a count badge and Refresh (`internal/web/ui/src/pages/organizer.tsx:253-258`); the Logger's are counters, Clear log and Refresh (`internal/web/ui/src/pages/logger.tsx:248-272`). Neither row context menu offers an export (`pages/organizer.tsx:420-443`, `pages/logger.tsx:354-395`).

## Classification
CAPABILITY GAP.

## Sizing note
`historyToCSV` (`internal/web/ui/src/lib/api.ts:180`) plus `downloadText` are the working precedent, including a deliberate decision about empty values (`lib/api.ts:121-123`). Note that precedent does *not* currently implement the Excel formula guard Burp's docs specify; if these exports are added, that guard is worth applying to all three rather than only the new two, since a note field is far more likely to start with `=` or `-` than a URL is.

## What an operator cannot do
Get saved exchanges or logged requests out of the tool. The Organizer's whole purpose is collecting evidence for a report, and its contents can only leave by hand.
acceptance_criteria: Both tables export the selection (or the whole table when nothing is selected) as CSV, reusing History's export path. The Excel formula guard Burp specifies for values starting with -, +, = or @ is applied, including retroactively to the History export.
close_reason: Implemented in 737497a: verified live in browser (annotation round-trip, capture filter save, CSV export with formula guard) and gated (go build/vet/test, bun check, 187 lib tests pass).

title: logger: entries cannot be annotated with a comment or highlight, and Entry.Note is unused
description:
## Claim
Logger entries cannot be annotated with a comment or a highlight, although `toollog.Entry` already carries an unused `Note` field.

## Burp-side evidence
`tools/logger/entries.html`, "Annotating log entries":
> "You can annotate log entries for later attention:
> To highlight an entry, click in the # column and choose a color from the drop-down menu.
> To leave a comment on an entry, double-click on the Comment column."

`tools/logger/filter/view.html` pairs it with a filter, which is what makes annotation useful rather than decorative:
> "**Filter by annotation** - Choose whether to show only items that have been annotated, either by a comment or highlight."

## burpsy-side evidence
The field exists on the record and is dead. `internal/toollog/toollog.go:102`:
```go
Note        string
```
It appears twice in the whole file (the struct field and nothing that writes it):
```
$ grep -c "Note" internal/toollog/toollog.go
2
```
It is absent from the wire projection — `toolLogEntry`, `internal/web/api_toolkit.go:835-854`, carries `id, tool, host, port, method, path, status, response_len, started_ms, duration_ms, error` and no note.

Consequently there is no annotation UI: the Logger columns are Age / Tool / Authority / Request / Status / Length / Time / Error (`internal/web/ui/src/pages/logger.tsx:130-196`), and the row context menu is copy-URL, copy-curl and two show-in-history actions (`pages/logger.tsx:354-395`). No highlight, no comment.

For contrast, the pattern exists elsewhere in the build: the Organizer has a highlight swatch row and a note textarea (`internal/web/ui/src/pages/organizer.tsx:498-527`), with `HIGHLIGHTS` / `HIGHLIGHT_TONE` already shared from `internal/web/ui/src/lib/types.ts`.

## Classification
CAPABILITY GAP. Partly a wiring job — the storage field is already there, unused.

## What an operator cannot do
Mark a logged request to come back to. On a log of a few thousand tool requests there is no way to flag the three that looked wrong, and no way to filter to them afterwards.
acceptance_criteria: A logged entry can be given a highlight colour and a comment, both projected on the wire and persisted for the life of the log, reusing the Organizer's existing highlight vocabulary. The table can filter to annotated entries.
close_reason: Implemented in 737497a: verified live in browser (annotation round-trip, capture filter save, CSV export with formula guard) and gated (go build/vet/test, bun check, 187 lib tests pass).

title: session: no session-handling tracer — nothing shows which rules and actions ran on a request
description:
## Claim
There is no session-handling tracer: nothing shows which rules and actions were applied to a request, or how the request changed at each step.

## Burp-side evidence
`settings/sessions/index.html`, "Session handling tracer":
> "The session handling tracer can help you when troubleshooting your session handling configuration. To view the tracer, click Open sessions tracer.
> The tracer shows a listing of every request that has been handled by the session handling functionality (that is, those requests where at least one session rule has been applied). For each request handled, the tracer shows **the sequence of rules and actions that were carried out. It also shows the changes made to the current request at each step in the sequence.** This information can help you to see whether your current rule configuration is achieving the required results."

Burp also states its cost, which is a design input here: "The session handling tracer imposes a processing and storage overhead on all affected HTTP requests. We recommend that you only use the tracer when troubleshooting issues with session handling rules." — i.e. it is opt-in, not always-on.

## burpsy-side evidence
Nothing records per-request rule application. `Coordinator.MatchingRule(host)` (`internal/session/session.go:942`) returns a rule and keeps no trace; `RunMacro` (`internal/session/session.go:1029`) returns the steps sent, the per-step results and a validity state to its caller but stores no history.

Extraction outcomes *are* logged, to the zap logger rather than to a readable surface — `Coordinator.logExtraction` (`internal/session/session.go:977`). That is diagnostics for whoever has the process log, not a tracer for the operator.

The only per-run feedback on the page is the single most recent "Run login now" result — `internal/web/ui/src/pages/session.tsx:566-587` builds `loginRows` from `loginResult`, and `:424` holds exactly one:
```ts
const [loginResult, setLoginResult] = useState<SessionLoginResponse | null>(null);
```
It covers one deliberately-triggered probe, reports outcome / rule / failed-step / validity (`pages/session.tsx:570-585`), and is replaced by the next run. It says nothing about the requests that flowed through the coordinator on their own.

Absence-grep with same-file positive control:
```
$ grep -rn "tracer\|Tracer" --include=*.go internal/session/ internal/web/
(no output)
$ grep -c "func " internal/session/session.go
43
$ grep -c "func " internal/web/api_session.go
24
```

## Classification
CAPABILITY GAP.

## Dependency
Most valuable after rules gain an action list (see the rule-actions issue) — tracing one hardcoded behaviour is worth much less than tracing an ordered sequence of actions, which is what makes a misconfiguration hard to see. Worth filing now because it is also the missing evidence trail for the cookie-jar and tools-scope issues: when a request unexpectedly carries or lacks a session, there is currently nothing to consult.

## What an operator cannot do
Debug a session rule that is not firing. There is no way to tell "the rule matched but the extraction found nothing" from "no rule matched this host" from "the rule fired and the target still rejected us", except by reading the process log.
acceptance_criteria: An opt-in tracer records, per request the coordinator handled, which rule matched and the sequence of steps taken with the change made to the request at each step, readable from the Session page. Off by default, with its overhead stated where it is enabled.
close_reason: Shipped as one unit (the recorded design said a tracer endpoint without a view repeats the e23c mistake). (1) internal/session/tracer.go: an opt-in bounded ring (200 entries, oldest dropped) on the Coordinator — off by default, one atomic load per handled request while off, per Burp's own overhead warning which the acceptance criteria took as the design input. Disabling KEEPS the recorded entries — the evidence is what the operator enabled the tracer to collect; a toggle that erased it would destroy the troubleshooting session on the way out. The entry reuses the rule's own []ActionRan walk (index, kind, label, detail, changed, skipped), so the tracer and the recovery report can never disagree about what ran. (2) The hook is HandleRecovery — Burp's 'every request where at least one session rule has been applied', so unmatched requests are not traced. (3) GET /api/session/trace (entries + enabled + capacity) and POST /api/session/trace/enable; ActionRan projected to lowercase with the kind spelled (set_cookie) — raw tags would say Index/Kind and the UI would read undefined. (4) The Session page's Tracer card: recording/off badge, Start/Stop with the overhead stated at the toggle, entries as identity + rule badge + outcome badge + the ordered action walk with each step's change/skip, and the capacity note. LIVE-VERIFIED: enabled over the API, the Run-login-now probe drove HandleRecovery, and the trace answered session · 127.0.0.1/account · 'trace me' · 'rule applied' with the walk showing set_cookie 'changed the request (set cookie traced=yes)'; the UI rendered the same entry as a badge'd row with the ordered action list; Stop tracing flipped the badge, toasted 'What it recorded is kept below', and the entry STAYED visible — the keep-on-disable contract observed. Tests: tracer_test.go 4/4 (off by default; handled traced and unmatched not; disable keeps entries and records nothing further; the ring is bounded and the snapshot stays oldest-first across a wrap). Gates: build/vet/gofmt clean, session+web green, tsc clean, bun test green, bundle+stylesheet rebuilt, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

comments.author: burpsy
comments.text: Claimed by the loop sweep, released after scoping with the design recorded. Shape: (1) an opt-in tracer on Coordinator — a bounded ring (say 200 entries) of {at, host, path, rule name, actions taken, extraction outcomes}, written from MatchingRuleFor/HandleResponse ONLY when enabled, so the per-response hot path pays nothing while the tracer is off (Burp's own overhead warning is the design input); (2) GET /api/session/trace + POST /api/session/trace/enable in the web layer; (3) a Tracer view on the Session page listing entries with the request identity and what changed. The existing logExtraction gives the extraction-outcome half today (zap-only); the trace should reuse its outcome naming. Deliverable is one unit with the UI — a tracer endpoint without a view repeats the e23c mistake. Session-epic adjacent (a09g).

title: intruder: no Auto-pause — an attack cannot stop itself when an expression appears in or disappears from a response
description:
Burp's Auto-pause pauses an attack when a chosen expression appears in — or goes missing from — a
response. burpsy has no equivalent.

Filed separately from the general "cannot stop an attack" issue because it is a distinct control with
its own configuration, but it is **blocked on that one**: there is nothing to pause until a running
attack has a pause mechanism.

## Burp-side evidence

`/root/burp-re/in/extract/resources/Documentation/burp/documentation/desktop/tools/intruder/configure-attack/settings.html`,
under **Auto-pause attack**:

> These settings automatically pause the attack when a specified expression appears in or is missing
> from a response.
>
> - Select **Enable auto-pause**.
> - Choose one of: **Pause if an expression in the list appears in a response** / **Pause if an
>   expression in the list is missing from a response**.
> - Add expressions to the list ...
> - Select the **Match type**: Simple string / Regex.
> - If required, enable **Case-sensitive match**.
>
> During the attack, Burp automatically pauses the attack if a response contains (or doesn't contain)
> the expressions. You can resume the attack at any time ... Once resumed, Burp will pause the attack
> each time a response meets the auto-pause condition.

## burpsy-side evidence

Absence grep:

    $ grep -rli "auto_pause|autopause" internal/intruder internal/web/api_tools.go internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx
    (no output)

Positive control from the same invocation over the same paths: `grep -rli "baseline" ...` →
`internal/intruder/engine_test.go`.

- `internal/web/api_tools.go:348-364` — `intruderRunReq` has no auto-pause field.
- `internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx:1043-1065` — the Settings tab has only the two grep fields.
- `internal/intruder/engine.go:89-101` — the per-response hook that would host this check
  (`Grep.run`) computes a match boolean and an extraction and returns; nothing can act on the result
  to halt the loop.

What exists and is *not* this: `intruder.RateLimit.WithAutoThrottle`
(`internal/web/api_tools.go:420-428`) slows the attack in response to configured HTTP statuses. That is
Burp's throttling, keyed on status, and it slows rather than pauses — it cannot key on response
content and it does not stop.

## Classification

CAPABILITY GAP.

## What an operator cannot do

Stop an attack automatically when it starts doing damage or when it has found what it was looking for.
The two cases Burp's docs are built around: a lockout page appearing mid-spray (the operator wants to
stop before locking every account), and a success indicator appearing (the operator wants to stop
rather than send the remaining 4,000 requests). Today the attack runs to its bound either way, and
because there is no manual stop either, both outcomes are unavoidable once launched.

## Sequencing

Do the manual pause/stop work first — a mechanism that can halt a running attack, and a report shape
that can say it was halted. Auto-pause is then a predicate evaluated in the same place `Grep.run`
already runs, plus its expression list and options. The expression-list plumbing overlaps with the
Grep - match arity issue; the two should share one list type rather than growing two.
acceptance_criteria: Auto-pause is configurable with an expression list, appears/missing mode, match type and case sensitivity, and a triggered condition actually pauses the attack with the report saying so.
close_reason: AutoPause predicate over the same bytes Grep.run reads, firing Control.Pause — the mechanism existed; this is the trigger. Appears mode = any expression matches; missing mode = none does (complement over ONE list). Simple strings quote-meta + case-fold unless case_sensitive; regex compiled as given; uncompilable expression refused 400 at the run endpoint (an auto-pause that silently never fires lies by omission). In-flight response collected whole; pause holds future enumerations (the same in-flight-window rule Control documents; fixtures run 1-wide to make the hold observable). Report carries auto_paused (attack-level atomic so ReArm-on-resume cannot erase the account of who pressed the button). Wire: intruderRunReq.auto_pause {expressions, missing, simple, case_sensitive}. Tests: appears halts (no NEW sends while paused — asserted on the sender counter, settled counts race by design), missing halts, case-sensitivity, regex-as-given, uncompilable refused, nil inert, wire round-trip auto_paused non-zero. Commit 0554b6d.

title: collaborator: mints one payload per click, with no batch generation and no id-only form
description:
## Claim
The Collaborator mints one payload per click with no way to generate several at once and no control over whether the server location is included.

## Burp-side evidence
`tools/collaborator/index.html`, "Generating payloads":
> "You can also generate multiple payloads at once in the Collaborator tab:
> Enter the number of Collaborator payloads that you want to generate in the **Payloads to generate** field.
> To include the full Collaborator server address in your payloads, select **Include Collaborator server location**. If this is not selected, only the Collaborator ID is included in your payloads.
> Click **Copy to clipboard** to copy the specified number of payloads.
> To access the payloads, paste them into a document."

`BURP_SUITE_UI_UX_SPECIFICATION.md` §4.7 lists a "Generate Payload" button as a Collaborator control.

## burpsy-side evidence
One mint per click, straight to the clipboard — `internal/web/ui/src/pages/collaborator.tsx:144-158`:
```tsx
<Button size="small" disabled={!s.configured || mint.isPending}
  onClick={() => mint.mutate(undefined, {
    onSuccess: (payload) => {
      void copyToClipboard(payload.address);
      toast.success(`Payload ${payload.address} copied`);
    },
```
The mutation takes no argument (`mint.mutate(undefined, …)`), so there is no count parameter on the wire, and the button is labelled "Copy payload" (`:157`) — singular by construction.

There is no bare-id form. The response field consumed is `payload.address` (`:150`), the full address; nothing renders or copies an id-only variant.

Minted payloads are counted but not listed for the interaction channel — the status card shows `s.payloads.length` as a metric (`pages/collaborator.tsx:180`) with no table. (The blind-XSS section below it *does* list its payloads with per-row copy, `pages/collaborator.tsx:228-251` — so the pattern to follow already exists on the same page.)

## Classification
CAPABILITY GAP.

## Sizing note
Smaller than it looks: the blind-XSS payload table on the same page (`pages/collaborator.tsx:228-251`) is the shape needed, and the mint endpoint would take a count. "Include server location" needs a decision on whether an id-only payload is meaningful for an interactsh-backed channel — with interactsh the correlation id is embedded in the subdomain, so an id without the domain may not be a usable payload here. If it is not, decline that half explicitly rather than shipping a toggle that changes nothing.

## What an operator cannot do
Prepare a batch of addresses before a test run — one per injection point across a form — without clicking mint and pasting once per payload, and without a list of what was minted to correlate against later.
acceptance_criteria: The operator can mint N payloads in one action and copy them all, and minted payloads for the interaction channel are listed with per-row copy as the blind-XSS section already does. Whether an id-only payload is meaningful for an interactsh channel is decided and, if not, declined in writing rather than shipped as a toggle.
close_reason: Batch payload minting: POST /api/collaborator/payload takes {"count": N} (absent=1, legacy client unchanged — response keeps the single address field plus full addresses/markers lists), bounded at 100 with a named refusal, batch shares the one registration and differs only by marker, hub records every payload so the page lists them all. UI: count input beside Copy payload, full list to clipboard. The id-only form was declined with reasoning on the issue: the marker IS the correlator and the address form is what makes it embeddable as a hostname — an id-only payload would force manual recombination and break the attribution contract the surface documents. Verified against the REAL public interactsh pool (live registration, real oast.online domain, single+batch=3 share domain, hub holds 4); mutations both caught live (count-ignored, ceiling-dropped); full web suite, tsc, 298 lib tests, dist, route+a11y gates green.

title: collaborator: interaction table has no protocol filter, search, annotation or mark-as-read
description:
## Claim
The Collaborator interaction table cannot be filtered by protocol, searched, or annotated, and interactions cannot be marked read.

## Burp-side evidence
`tools/collaborator/index.html`, "Viewing results":
> "Results are displayed in the table. You can perform the following actions to analyze the results:
> **Filter the table** - To filter the table by network protocol, click the HTTP, DNS, and SMTP buttons.
> **Search the table** - Click Search and enter an expression.
> **Annotate interactions** - Right-click any interaction and select Comment or Highlight.
> **Mark interactions as read** - Select the desired interactions then right-click and select Mark as read."

And the unread count is surfaced globally: "The number of unread interactions is displayed on the Collaborator tab label, making it easy for you to see interaction counts at a glance."

## burpsy-side evidence
The table is a bare `SimpleTable` with no controls — `internal/web/ui/src/pages/collaborator.tsx:284`:
```tsx
<SimpleTable headers={["#", "Type", "Client IP", "Payload", "Time", ""]}>
```
Rows render a type badge, IP, payload and time, plus an Open button (`pages/collaborator.tsx:285-301`). The only state the component holds is which row is expanded — `const [selected, setSelected] = useState<number | null>(null)` (`pages/collaborator.tsx:44`). No filter state, no search box, no context menu, no read/unread.

The columns themselves match `BURP_SUITE_UI_UX_SPECIFICATION.md` §4.7 ("Columns: Interaction ID, Type (DNS, HTTP, SMTP), Client IP, Time") — the data is there; the triage controls are not.

Protocol filtering has real values to filter on: the OOB client models four — `internal/oob/client.go:67`:
```go
// Protocol is "dns", "http", "smtp" or "ldap".
```
So a filter is not blocked on data. Note burpsy has one protocol more than Burp's three buttons (ldap), which the filter design should account for rather than hardcoding Burp's set.

## Classification
CAPABILITY GAP.

## Scoping note — what already works, do not redo
Minting, the 5-second auto-refresh (`internal/web/ui/src/lib/data.collab.ts:56,68,173`, tighter than Burp's 60s auto-poll), the detail pane with correlation id, client-IP interpretation and raw request (`pages/collaborator.tsx:307-335`), and the honest poll-semantics disclosure (`internal/web/api_collaborator.go:83-85`) are all in place. This issue is the table's triage controls only.

## What an operator cannot do
Work a channel that has collected volume. With a few hundred DNS interactions from a scan plus the handful of HTTP hits that actually prove a finding, there is no way to show only HTTP, search for the payload subdomain in question, or mark what has been reviewed.
acceptance_criteria: The interaction table can be filtered by protocol (covering all protocols the OOB client models, not just Burp's three), searched by expression, and annotated with a comment or highlight; interactions can be marked read and an unread count is visible without opening the page.
close_reason: Interaction table triage: protocol filter derived from the rows (covers dns/http/smtp/ldap — one more than Burp's three buttons), search over interaction_id/type/q_type/client_ip/payload plus the annotation, per-row mark-as-read + mark-all-read, per-interaction comment/highlight (inline annotate row: comment input + colour select), hide-read toggle, and an unread/all-read badge in the section heading. Read state and annotations persist in the workspace store (per-browser view state, like the Inspector dock — the channel is a subprocess-appended log nothing here owns); the unread count on the tool tab itself rides burpsy-react-ui-xvo's tab-attention work, with the in-page badge carrying it meanwhile. Verified live with real callbacks: minted a payload, resolved it so the public pool logged 3 DNS interactions; filter dns=3/http=0, search AAAA=2 / by comment=1, mark-read flips badge to 'all read', annotation survives reload. Commit 0d3ba46.

title: comparer: no hex view of the compared items
description:
## Claim
The Comparer has no hex view of the compared items, though the Decoder on the same build has one.

## Burp-side evidence
`tools/comparer.html`, "Results" — the controls in the results window:
> "There are various controls in the results window that help you to analyze the results:
> Sync views - Select this setting to scroll the two panels simultaneously.
> **Text** - View both items in text form.
> **Hex** - View both items in hex form."

## burpsy-side evidence
No view toggle on the page. The panes render text spans directly — `internal/web/ui/src/pages/comparer.tsx:95-108` (`Pane`, emitting `<span>` per segment), and the header actions are Swap and Compare only (`pages/comparer.tsx:253-265`).

The page's own badge asserts the granularity but not a view mode — `pages/comparer.tsx:255`: `<Badge>byte-level</Badge>`.

For contrast, the machinery exists one page over: the Decoder has a Text/Hex toggle (`internal/web/ui/src/pages/decoder.tsx:276-293`) backed by a local `hexDump` (`pages/decoder.tsx:39-55`) with a `MAX_HEX_BYTES` cap (`:37`) and a documented reason for the cap (`:33-36`).

## Why it matters on this page specifically
The diff is byte-level and its ops carry byte offsets — `byteSlice` at `pages/comparer.tsx:13-16` slices through a `TextEncoder` view precisely because "Ops carry byte offsets, so slicing has to go through the same byte view the server used". A byte-level diff whose only rendering is text is hard to read exactly where it matters: a difference in whitespace, a stray CR, a NUL, or a non-UTF-8 byte shows as nothing or as a replacement character. The padding glyph the panes use for alignment (`GAP_CHAR = "·"`, `:34`) is itself indistinguishable from a real middot in the data.

## Classification
CAPABILITY GAP.

## What an operator cannot do
Identify a whitespace-only or non-printable-byte difference between two responses — which on a byte-level comparer is the class of difference the tool is best placed to find.
acceptance_criteria: The Comparer offers a Text/Hex toggle that renders both panes as aligned hex with the diff highlighting preserved, so a whitespace-only or non-printable-byte difference is visible. Reuses the Decoder's dump approach including its size cap.
close_reason: Added a Text/Hex toggle to Comparer (mirroring Decoder's Braces/Hash toggle) backed by buildHexRows, which builds each side's hex+ASCII grid from the diff ops and that side's own real encoded bytes rather than the text pane's GAP_CHAR-padded strings, so a whitespace-only or non-printable-byte difference reads as a real distinct hex byte instead of nothing or the padding glyph. Hunk numbering matches buildSegments exactly, so hunk highlighting and jump-to-hunk work in hex mode. Capped at 8192 bytes/side, mirroring Decoder's hexDump cap. Unit-tested (comparer.test.ts) with a proven-fails-without-fix case (side-selection regression: 1/4 failed with 'Expected: 3, Received: 2' before restoring the fix, 4/4 after). E2E-verified with a new spec (e2e/specs/comparer-hex.spec.ts) against a real rebuilt burpsy: confirmed it fails (times out waiting for the Hex button) against the true pre-fix source, and passes against the fix. Scoped regression checks on the built fix: routes.spec.ts --grep comparer (1/1 pass), a11y.spec.ts --grep '#comparer' both themes (2/2 pass, 0 violations). Did not run the full e2e-ui.sh suite per coordinator guidance — it carries four pre-existing failures unrelated to this change (smsz, 92o5, q4i0), all reproduced against HEAD. Gate green: tsc --noEmit, targeted bun test, build (only dist/app.js diffed), go build ./...

title: comparer: only two overwritable slots — no item tables, so each send-to destroys a side
description:
## Claim
The Comparer holds only two overwritable slots — there are no item tables, so a new "Send to Comparer" destroys a side rather than adding to a list.

## Burp-side evidence
`tools/comparer.html`, "Carrying out comparisons":
> "Right-click each message and select Send to Comparer. You can send a message from anywhere in Burp. Go to the Comparer tab. **The messages are listed in the two item tables.** Select the two messages you want to compare."
> "Note: The two item tables each display a list of all the messages that you have sent to Comparer. You need to select an item from each table. To sort the contents of the table, click on any table header."

And the controls that manage those lists:
> "**Paste** - Add an item from the clipboard. **Load** - Add an item from a file. **Remove** - Delete the highlighted item. **Clear** - Delete all items in the list."

## burpsy-side evidence
Two scalar slots in component state — `internal/web/ui/src/pages/comparer.tsx:119-122`:
```ts
const [a, setA] = useState("");
const [b, setB] = useState("");
```
A hand-off overwrites — `pages/comparer.tsx:139-149`:
```ts
useEffect(() => {
  if (!slots.a) return;
  setA(slots.a);
  setComparerSlot("a", "");
}, [slots.a, setComparerSlot]);
```
The store carries one string per side (`sendToComparer(exchange, slot)` at `internal/web/ui/src/lib/actions.ts:193`, menu entries at `:368-369`), so the third send-to a slot replaces the first with no record that it existed.

The rendered surface per side is one editor plus a message-id Load — `pages/comparer.tsx:214-247`. There is no list, and no Remove or Clear.

`Load` exists in a different sense than Burp's: it fetches stored message bytes by numeric id (`loadSlot`, `pages/comparer.tsx:170-187`) rather than adding a file to a list.

## Classification
CAPABILITY GAP.

## Not the word-level issue
Distinct from `burpsy-react-ui-mwq` (Comparer has no word-level diff mode), which is the declined-and-disclosed granularity claim. This is about how many items the tool can hold.

## What an operator cannot do
Compare pairs out of a set. The Intruder use case Burp's own docs lead with — "compare large responses with different lengths that you have identified in an Intruder attack" — means sending five or six candidates over and trying pairs; here each send-to costs the operator whichever side they aimed at.
acceptance_criteria: Each side holds a list of items that send-to appends to, with per-item remove and a clear-all, and the comparison runs on the selected item from each list. Sending an exchange to a side no longer discards what was there.
close_reason: Burp's item tables are live: 'The messages are listed in the two item tables. Select the two messages you want to compare.' Each side is now a LIST. (1) The sender contract is unchanged — every send-to across six pages still calls the same one-shot hand-off; the Comparer consumes arrivals into its list instead of into the editor, labels each by its first line (the request/status line, what an operator scanning two tables reads), and selects it. Selecting loads the editor; the list is the memory, the editor the working copy, edits do not rewrite stored items — the deal Burp's own tables offer. (2) store.ts: ComparerItem with monotonic per-session ids (remove-then-add cannot alias a stale React key), addComparerItem (append, never replace), removeComparerItem (exactly the named item), clearComparerItems (one side, never both). (3) The page: each slot renders its item table — one row per sent message with a size column, an at-a-glance selected state, per-item Remove (deselecting and emptying the editor when it removes the selected one), and Burp's Clear per side. LIVE-VERIFIED on a seeded console with three distinguishable exchanges: two sends to one side left BOTH items in the table with the newest selected; selecting from each list and pressing Compare produced a real diff (Verdict different, Deleted 124 B only in A, one hunk drawn in both panes); removing the unselected item left the rest in order; removing the SELECTED item cleared the list AND emptied the editor back to its placeholder. One mid-drive confusion (my row indices read the newest-first table backwards) resolved as exactly that — every send landed correctly; the product was right. Mutations, observed: add-replaces FAILs, clear-wipes-both FAILs — both killed. Tests: comparer-items.test.ts 4/4 (append, exact remove without reorder, side independence, monotonic ids). Gates: tsc clean, bun test green, bundle+stylesheet rebuilt, go build/vet/gofmt clean, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

title: repeater: the Protocol override cannot force HTTP/2 — only auto or force HTTP/1.1
description:
